STRATEGIC VISION & GROUP PRIORITIES

MESSAGE FROM THE CHAIRMAN & CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER

CATHERINE MACGREGOR Chief Executive Of ˱cer JEAN-PIERRE CLAMADIEU Chairman of the Board of Directors

Based on your observations, what dynamics are transforming the global energy landscape?

Finally, while public opinion seems less sensitive to climate issues, the effects of global warming are all around us, and 2025 ranked among the three hottest years on record.

Against a backdrop of global upheaval, what pathway is the energy transition taking?

Jean-Pierre Clamadieu: 2025 marked a tipping point with far‑reaching consequences for governments and businesses alike. The hardening of the balance of power between partners was unprecedented, while governments and businesses were caught off-guard by the questioning of rules and the weakening of institutions previously considered to be stable. These geopolitical tensions incorporate energy issues now more than ever, as we are seeing with the situation in the Middle East.

Catherine MacGregor: In this geopolitical context, energy is clearly a central issue. The energy transition is accelerating in response to government needs to secure reliable, abundant and low-carbon energy. In this sense, renewable energies bolster a country’s sovereignty by reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels.

The AI race between the United States and China is fueling remarkable growth in electricity demand, while oil and gas are once again becoming a major issue in US foreign policy. This growth is being driven by a steady decline in the cost of battery-related renewables and, for gas, by the strong momentum of LNG rollout, particularly from the United States. In Europe, awareness of external dependencies is encouraging a return to local content.

Energy players are at the forefront of these changes, demonstrating their resilience as the sector continues to grow and as investment needs open up new prospects. They are adapting to rapid and sometimes unpredictable changes in legal frameworks, which can lead to some projects being slowed down or reconsidered due to lack of visibility or stability.

Our Group is a major player in this transition, which is nevertheless progressing with different dynamics and drivers in different regions. In the United States, the term energy “addition” is used rather than “transition”, and renewables remain an effective response to increasing energy demand. In China, the energy transition is ˱rst and foremost a strategic lever, as demonstrated by the intensity of R&D efforts and the unrivaled pace of deployment of new renewable capacities. India, like other countries in the Middle East, is also setting concrete and ambitious targets. More than ever, Europe's trajectory is based on a strategic imperative: strengthening its sovereignty and sustaining its competitiveness, while maintaining the course set by its climate goals.

At a time when demand for electricity is being driven by AI players and data centers, we have con˱rmed our position as the global leader in PPAs, with 4.8 GW contracted over the year with major clients such as Meta, Google and Apple. 2025 was also an important year in Belgium, where we ˱nalized the agreement with the Belgian government on nuclear waste and made major operational advances.

“Our robust utility model means we can face the future with con ˱dence”

Where does Europe stand in its energy transition?

A clear sign of our ˱nancial strength, at the end of the year our market capitalization exceeded €50 billion, and has strengthened. LINK 2025, the special edition of ENGIE's employee shareholding plan launched to mark the brand's 10 th

anniversary, was a huge success, pointing to the support and con ˱dence of our teams in the Group's strategy.

Jean-Pierre Clamadieu: In 2025, for the ˱rst time, the majority of the European Union's electricity generation came from renewable sources. This illustrates the importance of the efforts made over the last decade to make electricity generation greener.

Our robust utility model proved its worth, giving us a unique positioning and enabling us to face the future with con˱dence.

What can you tell us about the agreement signed with CK Infrastructure Holdings Limited to acquire UK Power Networks?

Europe boasts major assets that can strengthen its energy sovereignty. These range from a highly interconnected grid, an integrated market and an energy mix that capitalize on the strengths of each region, from Scandinavian hydroelectricity to offshore wind and solar power in the South. It is now taking stock of these assets and capitalizing on them, while strengthening its infrastructure network.

Signi˱cant progress is still to be made in electri˱cation – particularly in industry and transport – but also in the development of a competitive green molecule offering, which is essential if the European Union is to achieve the 2050 targets it has set itself.

Jean-Pierre Clamadieu: This acquisition represents an important step in the Group's transformation. We are signi ˱cantly increasing our presence in electricity infrastructures, which are an essential pillar of the energy transition. This strengthens the Group's regulated pro˱le, while offering us opportunities for growth in a sector and a country with considerable needs.

What conditions are needed to guarantee an affordable energy transition for citizens and businesses alike?

Catherine MacGregor: The acquisition of UK Power Networks is proof of the ambition we expressed nearly two years ago to develop our electrical distribution business. The fact that this acquisition is in the UK – a country that has set itself a clear course for decarbonization and electri ˱cation – means we will bene˱t from a particularly mature regulatory framework that values performance and customer satisfaction.

UK Power Networks is a "best-in-class" all-round electricity distributor, serving 8.5 million customers in London, the East and the South East of England. It stands out for the scope and quality of its network, for its operational and economic performance recognized by the regulator, and for the expertise of its 6,500 employees. Thanks to this acquisition, the Group is now positioned across all growth drivers of the energy transition.

Catherine MacGregor: We are convinced that only a pragmatic approach based on an energy mix combining electrons and molecules will enable us to drive an energy transition that is affordable for everyone. This model is based on the development of renewable electric energies combined with ˳exibility solutions such as battery storage. It enables us to supply all our customers with abundant green electricity that is available in the right place at the right time. The guarantee of affordable energy also relies on a system dependent on gas, which is essential for sectors that cannot be electri˱ed. The transition in the gas sector continues, with biomethane solutions today and hydrogen in the future. All these energy vectors will be rolled out thanks to the networks and interconnections that balance our energy system.

Is ENGIE's strategy still aligned with the Group's purpose?

For all these reasons, energy policies and regulatory frameworks must be stable, and we must play a decisive role in developing competitive local industrial sectors.

Jean-Pierre Clamadieu: Yes, absolutely, and the Board of Directors pays very close attention to this. The Group's transformation continues, and our strategy remains closely aligned with our purpose, reconciling economic performance with positive societal impact.

And ˱nally, our integrated model allows us to offer the most appropriate solutions in the countries where we operate. To ensure accessibility and support an affordable energy transition, we are constantly boosting the competitiveness and performance of all our entities.

How did ENGIE deliver on its strategy in 2025?

In 2025, we celebrated 10 years of the ENGIE brand; an excellent opportunity to remind ourselves that 2015 was a decisive turning point: that of the Paris Agreement when the climate emergency was clearly recognized by political leaders and company executives.

Catherine MacGregor: By clarifying and consolidating the scope of our Global Business Units, our new organization strengthened our collective ef ˱ciency, and we can be proud of what we achieved.

ENGIE is continuing to follow this trajectory and at the 2025 Shareholders’ Meeting, we presented a broader climate strategy with more ambitious targets. We have integrated climate change adaptation measures, in addition to the mitigation measures, which is essential if we are to ensure the Group's long-term viability at a time of heightened risk. The challenge is to ensure the resilience of our assets, our supply chains and the health and safety of our people.

As regards renewable energies, we reached our target of 50 GW of installed capacity and stepped up our pace in storage projects. We are now positioned as a benchmark player in the industry. At the same time, we made progress on electricity infrastructures, particularly in Latin America, and continued to decarbonize gas, injecting 14.5 TWh of biomethane into the French gas network over the year. And, because the transition also happens at the local level, we continued to expand in

At a time when some players are scaling back their climate ambitions, our Group is maintaining its goal of achieving Net Zero Carbon by 2045 and is providing itself with the means to do so!

“ENGIE's purpose, or raison d'être , is to act to accelerate the transition to a carbon-neutral economy through low-energy solutions that are more respectful of the environment. With the growing market share of intermittent renewable power generation, the power generation system is facing new and mounting strain and a need for ˳exible resources. Thermal gas generation, battery storage and pumped storage help meet peak electricity demand and provide ˳exibility on various timescales. The Group is one of the leading power producers in Europe, notably supplying grid ˳exibility solutions via its gas-˱red power plants (15.8 GW in Europe in 2025). It also invests in the development of battery capacities to bring the necessary ˳exibility to the electricity grid (4.7 GW worldwide in 2025).

• Energy supply and management

The Group is active across the entire energy transition value chain and its integrated model enables it to create more value and enhances its resilience. ENGIE's commitment to accelerating the energy transition is best demonstrated by its commitment to achieve Net Zero Carbon (1) by 2045. By reliably providing affordable and accessible energy to all its customers, ENGIE is stepping up to its role of ful ˱lling an essential public service mission for society. The energy value chain consists of production, ˳exible power generation solutions (including thermal power plants (1) and batteries), transportation via centralized and decentralized energy networks, gas and electricity supply, and, lastly, energy management, which links each of these stages for optimization purposes:

• Production

Production includes renewable electricity (centralized and decentralized), nuclear power (centralized), in which the Group is a leader in Belgium, renewable gas (biomethane (1) , green hydrogen (1) ), production of heating and cooling, energy for industrial customers (distributed solar, geothermal, heat pumps, boilers, biomass (1) , etc.) and water from seawater desalination (1) . With 57.2 GW of installed renewable energy and storage capacity worldwide (1) in 2025, ENGIE is the number one wind and solar energy company in France and the second-largest developer in Europe. Worldwide, ENGIE supplies gas and electricity to almost 200,000 businesses and has nearly 20 million contracts with residential and small business customers. In Europe, ENGIE is one of the top gas and electricity sellers and one of the top gas importers (2) . In France, ENGIE is the historic leader of gas marketing and the second-largest supplier of electricity. In Belgium, through its subsidiary Electrabel, ENGIE is the leading supplier of electricity and natural gas (3) . ENGIE is also a global leader in long-term green corporate Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs), with 4.8 GW signed in 2025 ( Corporate Power Purchase Agreement – Corporate PPA (1) ). For the purposes of energy management, the Group's teams connect its assets to markets and customers.

1.1.2 History and development of the Company

The Company is the result of the merger of SUEZ with Gaz de France, following the decisions of the Ordinary and Extraordinary Shareholders' Meetings of Gaz de France and SUEZ of July 16, 2008. The merger took effect on July 22, 2008.

private sector. On July 22, 2008, Gaz de France absorbed SUEZ in a merger which entailed transferring the majority of the Company's share capital to the private sector. The new Company took the name GDF SUEZ.

SUEZ itself was the result of the merger in 1997 of Compagnie de Suez and Lyonnaise des Eaux. SUEZ became an international industrial and services group whose objective was to meet essential requirements in electricity, gas, energy and industry services, water and waste management. On July 9, 2007, SUEZ completed its takeover bid for all outstanding shares in Electrabel.

Gaz de France was initially incorporated in 1946 as a French public industrial and commercial enterprise ( Établissement public à caractère industriel et commercial ). It became a limited liability company with a 99-year term under French Act No. 2004-803 of August 9, 2004 on the public service of electricity and gas and electricity and gas companies (amending French Act No. 46-628 of April 8, 1946).

On July 7, 2005, Gaz de France publicly ˳oated its shares on the stock market. The Company's shares were ˱rst listed on July 7, 2005.

The deregulation of European energy markets in the early 1990s accelerated the international development of both Gaz de France and SUEZ, which progressively expanded their activities beyond their respective traditional markets, both in Europe and the rest of the world. This development continued with GDF SUEZ.

Energy markets continue to undergo rapid development, with a growing need for ˳exible solutions to guarantee the energy system's stability, as renewable energies become a main source of production and customer demand for carbon‑free energy increases. Consequently, in order to capitalize on these opportunities and draw full value from its integrated model, ENGIE adjusted the scope of its GBU in February 2025.

1.2.1.3 Centralized and local infrastructure

Intermittent and storable energy production, combined with ˳exibility solutions, relies on both centralized and local infrastructures for transmission and distribution. This is an important element of ENGIE’s integrated model. With regard to centralized infrastructure, the Group’s strategy consists of making sure that gas infrastructure operates ef˱ciently, adapting it to the rise of biomethane and hydrogen, and developing electrical infrastructure worldwide. The energy transition will require massive investment in electricity

networks around the world over the coming years, as they are an enabler for decarbonizing (1) the energy system. By 2030, the Group plans to have installed 10,000 km of power transmission lines (1) in Latin America. With regard to local infrastructures, the Group is focusing its development on urban heating and cooling networks, energy infrastructures at industrial sites and charging stations for electric vehicles, with the aim of managing 550, 250 and 25,000 of these respectively by 2030.

In terms of energy management, the Group optimizes the value of its energy, gas, renewable energies and storage assets, and manages portfolio risks across all its markets, thereby contributing to competitiveness and enabling the Group to fully deploy its integrated model.

The gas and electricity supply business involves selling energy. In all supply markets, ENGIE’s aim is to become a reliable, trusted partner and to support customers through the energy transition. To this end, the Group's priority is to market more and more green energy contracts with digital solutions including consumption management. By 2030, it aims to sell 300 TWh of electricity worldwide.

• managing risk and increasing revenues through portfolio effects and market optimization . In practical terms, this means streamlining the production, transmission and supply of energy by combining the Group's generation assets with storage and ˳exibility solutions, and linking these assets to end-customers via the marketing of electricity or gas to homes and businesses;

• industrial synergies . Economies of scale and standardization efforts create industrial synergies that improve process ef ˱ciency, reduce costs and mitigate operational risks (rationalized purchasing, pooled support functions, etc.). ENGIE launched the Global Enterprise Transformation (GET) program to accelerate ERP system standardization, the pooling of support functions and process ef˱ciency. Similarly, the standardization and sharing of expertise, particularly in the renewable energies sector, have led to signi˱cant ef˱ciency gains. For example, engineering skills in India have been insourced. This move was accompanied by the sharing of expertise at regional level, to support the development of 30 projects in the AMEA region (increasing negotiating power with Chinese EPC contractors).

The Group’s determination to be the best energy transition utility requires it to continue improving in the various levers that support its activities. The most important of these areas

Logically, the Group’s organization follows the energy value chain, from production to supply, and is composed of the following entities:

• the support functions , which operate in each geographic area (regional hubs) and at the individual country level. They have a key role in terms of support for the Global Business Units' activities and the development of synergies;

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

The organization operates based on a matrix set up between the business line entities and the functional departments, broken down into geographic areas.

• the Group’s functional departments , which oversee support functions in support of Executive Management and in coordination with the four GBU. They draw up and roll out Group policies and oversee ˱nancial and non-˱nancial performance;

The four GBU are responsible for their results at the global level and the implementation of the strategy within their respective business segments. This means that, within their respective scopes and the framework established by Executive Management (1) , each GBU is responsible for:

• de ˱ning the development strategy, making decisions and arbitrating on investments;

• managing industrial assets, operational excellence, safety and security;

To contribute to the decarbonization of cities, industrial sites and buildings, the Local Energy Infrastructures GBU develops and operates decentralized low-carbon infrastructures. More speci ˱cally, the GBU’s activities are divided into three main categories: local energy networks (particularly urban heating and cooling networks, electric and natural gas charging stations for vehicles (GNV) for low-carbon mobility), on-site energy production (heating, cooling and power production using solar panels, energy storage, etc.) and energy performance and management services (consulting, engineering and energy performance services) (see Section 1.3.3).

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

• managing performance processes, resources, expertise and the rollout of digital tools.

The operating activities in the countries report to the corresponding GBU.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

The Renewables & Flex Power GBU comprises centralized production activities and activities supporting ˳exibility. More speci˱cally, this GBU develops and operates solar, onshore and offshore wind and hydroelectric power generation assets, as well as ˳exibility assets including electricity storage assets (notably batteries) and thermal assets (such as Combined Cycle Gas Turbines or CCGTs), in order to supply more green and smart electrons (see Section 1.3.1).

To optimize the operation of the Group’s assets and supply all customers with reliable, sustainable energy, the Supply & Energy Management GBU comprises energy supply activities for large companies, industries and local authorities (BtoB) and smalland medium-sized businesses and individuals (BtoC), as well as energy management activities. More speci ˱cally, energy management activities involve managing the risks associated with energy volume ˳ows (production and sales), and consequently optimizing market assets. These activities also include offering energy management solutions to support the decarbonization of the Group’s activities and those of its customers (see Section 1.3.4).

networks, underground gas storage (1) and lique ˱ed natural gas (LNG) (1) terminals, as well as power transmission lines. It is also responsible for deploying the production of green molecules such as biomethane, green hydrogen and e‑molecules (see Section 1.3.2).

Strategy and organization

1.2.4.2 Description of support functions and geographical structure

An Executive Vice President, who is a member of the Executive Committee, is responsible for overseeing the geographic areas as a whole and the Group's transformation.

The support functions contribute to the Group's performance by supporting the performance of the GBU and the operating entities. They are managed by the Group HQ’s corporate functional departments and are structured regionally and nationally.

In addition to managing the various countries, the Transformation & Geographies Department is also responsible for:

• supervising and managing the Group's transformation projects;

• supervising and supporting the Group's industrial projects;

The Group's functional departments are responsible, within their respective areas, for drawing up and rolling out Group policies and overseeing ˱nancial and non-˱nancial performance. They are organized into ˱ve units:

• Corporate Secretariat, Governance, Legal & Ethics, Public Affairs, and Communications, Safety;

• Finance, Environment, Social and Governance (ESG), and Procurement;

• Data, Digital & IT, Strategy, and Research & Innovation;

• Human Resources;

• Transformation & Geographies.

• all activities relating to the health and safety of individuals (employees, temporary workers and subcontractors) and ensuring that industrial assets are safe to use, based on targets set by the Group in this area (No Life at Risk – No Mind at Risk – No Asset at Risk, see Section 3.1.3.2.6 Health & safety of employees and temporary workers, Section 3.1.3.3 Workers in the value chain (excluding energy) and Section 3.2.1.2 Prevention and mitigation measures for priority human rights risks).

Stronger and structured coordination of the division at Group level ensures that the processes deliver good operational ef ˱ciency and that Group policies are properly implemented.

Each of these areas is overseen by an Executive Vice President, who is a member of the Executive Committee (see Section 4.1.3 Executive Management).

Geographically, the support functions are organized by country and coordinated at regional level. These functions are responsible for supporting the GBU in each country, under the coordination of the country manager and regional coordinators.

In addition, ENGIE operates its own business. The number of consolidated entities will be around 2,400 by the end of 2025. text:

With regard to thermal power production, ENGIE has developed and is currently deploying an ambitious program to improve its ˳eet’s technical performance, aimed at equipping turbines with the best available technologies (where economically viable), to ensure maximum ef˱ciency, enable ˳exible operation (in line with market requirements and in complementarity with renewable activities), and reduce CO₂ emissions per MWh produced.

Finally, in several European countries where ENGIE is present - notably Italy, Belgium, Germany and Poland, as well as in certain markets under development such as Spain and the Netherlands - the authorities have introduced or are preparing to deploy capacity remuneration mechanisms. The aim of these systems is to ensure that supply and demand are matched, and to guarantee security of supply. They structure the investment signals for ˳exible assets such as battery storage, pump-turbine facilities, hydropower, ˳exible thermal resources and, where appropriate, demand response, thereby in˳uencing the valuation of ENGIE's portfolios in these countries.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

1.3.1.2.3 Offshore wind activities through Ocean Winds (OW)

In Belgium , ENGIE completed the construction of a new combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT) power plant in Flémalle. This latest generation power plant, with a capacity of 875 MW, bene ˱ts from the capacity remuneration mechanism introduced in Belgium to ensure security of supply following the decrease in the country's nuclear capacity. It should also be noted that the majority of ENGIE’s existing gas-˱red power plants in Belgium have been contracted under the Belgian capacity remuneration mechanism for the coming years.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

In the rest of Europe (excluding France), ENGIE manages a portfolio of thermal generation assets with installed capacity of 13.7 GW in ˱ve countries ( Belgium, the Netherlands, Italy, Portugal and Spain ). This includes the Group's power plants and the decentralized assets of industrial customers.

Ocean Winds (OW) is a joint venture created in 2019 by EDP Renováveis and ENGIE, combining ˱xed and ˳oating wind assets and projects, mainly in Europe. At the end of 2025, the joint venture operated an installed capacity of 2.8 GW (1.8 GW in the United Kingdom, 0.5 GW in Belgium, 0.4 GW in France and 0.03 GW in Portugal). Construction was under way on two offshore wind projects in 2025, including 0.6 GW in France and 0.4 GW in Poland.

Regulatory changes

Ocean Winds' offshore developments have been affected by the tightening of the U.S. regulatory environment, with the federal suspension of several projects under construction, that are subject to permit re-evaluation.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

The thermal production market in Europe is accelerating its transition to less carbon-intensive energy generation. Following the enactment of the European Green Deal, the European Commission has proposed targets to accelerate the reduction of CO 2 emissions between now and 2030. Various European countries have started to phase out electricity production from coal, and some have committed to fully decarbonized power generation by 2035.

In light of these changes, ENGIE has factored in a four-year delay for its offshore wind projects, and has scaled back its growth ambitions for onshore renewable capacities, in order to adapt its development strategy to the stricter regulatory environment. Under these circumstances, projects are subject to signi˱cant delays and higher costs.

Today, natural gas power plants play a key role in ensuring security of supply and offering the long-term ˳exibility needed for power systems, as a complement to wind and solar installations.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

This vital role underlines the importance of remuneration mechanisms for electricity producers, and calls for accelerating the study and development of decarbonization solutions for this type of ˳exibility (such as green fuels or carbon capture), to enable them to reconcile security of supply with decarbonization.

However, as they are located close to major U.S. consumption centers, the projects will bene˱t from the expected growth in overall energy demand in the United States, and particularly from the increase in demand for green energy. The power purchase agreements for these projects should therefore make them pro˱table, before the ˱nal investment decision is made. Ocean Winds is continuing its dialogue with the authorities and stakeholders to secure the operating environment.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

1.3.1.3 Activities in North America

Regulatory changes

North America is a priority market for ENGIE’s growth in renewable energy, with a large proportion of assets contracted to Commercial and Industrial (C&I) customers through corporate PPAs.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

In 2025, the political and regulatory framework for renewable energy activities underwent signi ˱cant change. For example, the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act", signed into law on July 4, 2025, provides for the elimination of the main support mechanisms for renewable energies and the withdrawal of several key provisions of the In˳ation Reduction Act, adopted under the previous administration. This implies a reduction in federal funding and the introduction of new constraints such as stricter rules relating to Foreign Entities of Concern (FEOC). The gradual end of the ITC (Investment Tax Credit/PTC - Production Tax Credit) regime and the introduction of measures aimed at relocating part of the industrial value chain to the United States also make the environment less favorable.

At end-2025, ENGIE managed a portfolio of 11.7 GW of renewable production and battery assets in North America. This portfolio consists of 4.2 GW of onshore wind (3.5 GW in the United States and 0.7 GW in Canada), 3.7 GW of solar in the United States and 3.8 GW of battery storage in the United States. The vast majority of this operational portfolio is located in ˱ve areas: ERCOT (Electric Reliability Council of Texas), SPP (Southwest Power Pool), PJM (Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Maryland) and MISO (Midcontinent Independent System Operator) in the United States and in Ontario (Canada). In 2025, ENGIE commissioned more than 2 GW (1.6 GW of batteries, 0.5 GW of solar and 0.3 GW of onshore wind).

ENGIE owns and operates the West Windsor 126 MW combined cycle natural gas power plant in Ontario, Canada . In addition, ENGIE holds a 35% stake in EcoElectrica, a 534 MW natural gas combined cycle power plant in Puerto Rico .

text:
Presentation of the Group

Description of the Group's activities at December 31, 2025

1.3.1.4 Activities in South America

Two of ENGIE’s ˱ve key markets are located in South America, where the Group has strong positions with 12.7 GW of hydropower (mainly in Brazil), 3.7 GW of onshore wind, 3 GW of solar power and 0.4 GW of battery storage.

ENGIE also has thermal activities in Chile and Peru . In Chile , ENGIE has a large thermal network in the north representing a total of 1.3 GW. The Group operates a diversi ˱ed portfolio of combined cycle or open cycle natural gas power plants, coal units that will be phased out (˱nalization in 2027) or converted to natural gas, and gas turbines and diesel engines.

In South America, ENGIE operates and develops its power generation activities mainly through long-term PPAs (power purchase agreements) entered into with electricity distributors, and through bilateral contracts signed directly with commercial and industrial customers. This model offers robust economic visibility and supports the competitive development of the Renewable and Flex Power GBU’s portfolio in the region.

As part of this effort, the Group is concentrating on converting the IEM unit at Mejillones to natural gas, while some of the infrastructure at the Tocopilla site will be reused to house a synchronous condenser, thereby contributing to the security of supply in Chile.

In Peru , ENGIE operates 2 GW in power plants, with natural gas- ˱red combined cycle power plants in Chilca, as well as diesel power plants in Ilo.

In Mexico, ENGIE operates gas- ˱red cogeneration (1) plants with a combined capacity of nearly 300 MW.

Regulatory changes

In Brazil , ENGIE operates 12.4 GW of hydropower, 2.5 GW of onshore wind and 1.6 GW of solar power. In 2025, ENGIE commissioned the Assú Sol solar farm and the Serra do Assuruá wind farm in Brazil, the largest in its global portfolio. They each have a capacity of 0.8 GW. These projects illustrate the Group's ability to develop large-scale infrastructure while supporting local employment and social initiatives for the bene ˱t of surrounding communities.

ENGIE Brasil Participações Ltda (EBP, 100% ENGIE subsidiary), holds 68.71% of the share capital of ENGIE Brasil Energia (EBE), which is responsible for the centralized electricity production and transportation business. EBP has a 40% interest in Energia Sustentavel do Brasil Participações S.A., which owns the Jirau hydropower power plant (3.7 GW).

In Chile , through its 60%-owned subsidiary ENGIE Energia Chile (EECL), ENGIE has 1.5 GW of renewable capacity, including 0.5 GW of solar power, 0.7 GW of onshore wind power and 0.4 GW of battery storage, and 0.05 GW of hydropower.

In 2025, Brazil's regulatory framework changed signi ˱cantly with the reform of the electricity market (Preliminary Law no. 1.300, published in May 2025), which will accelerate the opening up of the free market and rede˱ne support mechanisms. This reform provides for a gradual end to reductions in transmission and distribution tariffs for renewable energies, now limited to contracts registered before December 31, 2025. It also provides for changes to the management and compensation systems for production limits (curtailment). For ENGIE, these changes modify the economic conditions applicable to future projects and require an adjustment of development strategies to take account of the new pricing and operating framework.

In Mexico , the Group operates 1 GW (0.8 GW from solar power and 0.2 GW from onshore wind).

In Peru , ENGIE, through ENGIE Energia Peru (61.77%-owned by ENGIE), operates 0.3 GW of hydropower capacity, 0.3 GW of onshore wind, 0.1 GW of solar capacity and 0.03 GW of battery storage. The Punta Lomitas wind farm is the largest in the country and has taken over the Power Purchase Agreement from the Ilo21 coal- ˱red power plant that ceased to operate.

1.3.1.5 Activities in Asia, Middle East and Africa

ENGIE operates 3.9 GW of capacity in the region, including 1.7 GW from solar power, 2 GW from onshore wind power, and 0.2 GW of battery storage.

In India , ENGIE holds an installed capacity portfolio of around 1.3 GW in renewable energy, including 1 GW solar and 0.3 GW onshore wind. In Malaysia , ENGIE has 0.1 GW of solar power. In Australia , ENGIE holds a portfolio of 0.1 GW of solar, 0.2 GW of onshore wind and 0.2 GW of battery storage. The Group also operates several gas power plants with a total capacity of 723 MW. These plants contribute ˳exibility to the Australian system and enables ENGIE to take advantage of arbitrage opportunities on the markets.

Following the strategic realignment and the sale of assets in Bahrain and Kuwait, at the end of 2025 ENGIE operated a total of 23.7GW of thermal power production capacity in Saudi Arabia (7.5 GW), the United Arab Emirates (9.7 GW), Oman (2.7 GW), and Qatar (3.8 GW). Desalination plants in operation or under construction in these four countries represent a production capacity of nearly 5.4 million m 3 of water per day. The business portfolio and relationships with local stakeholders enable the Group to extend long-term agreements and strengthen their contribution to the Group’s results. For example, operation of the Shuweihat (1.2 GW) and Umm Al Nar (1.5 GW) power plants in the United Arab Emirates will be extended from 2027 for 2 and 15 years, respectively.

Finally, in Africa, ENGIE operates assets in Egypt (0.9 GW onshore wind), Morocco (0.4 GW onshore wind), and South Africa (0.6 GW solar, 0.25 GW onshore wind). In South Africa, ENGIE also holds a minority stake in two open-cycle diesel “peak” power plants, representing a total capacity of 1 GW. In addition, a desalination plant is currently under construction in Morocco , with a planned capacity of 100,000 m³ of water per day.

ENGIE has held a strong position in the Gulf Cooperation Council countries for many years. 1.3.2.1 Purpose and Strategy

The Networks GBU is responsible for developing, operating and maintaining gas networks (distribution and transport networks, storage and LNG terminals) and electricity networks. It is also responsible for renewable gas production (biomethane, hydrogen).

The business model for ENGIE’s gas infrastructure and electricity networks is, with one exception (TAG network, see Section 1.3.2.3), mainly regulated. The regulations that will apply to hydrogen infrastructure developments carried out by the relevant ENGIE subsidiaries are currently being de ˱ned.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

ENGIE is the leading gas network operator in Europe, and has 8,000 km of power lines in operation, under construction or under development in South America. ENGIE is also the second-largest producer of biomethane in France.

Electricity and gas networks are key to the energy transition:

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

• gas, which is gradually being greened through the development of renewable gases (biomethane, hydrogen, emethane), is an essential vector in the energy transition;

Activity relating to biomethane remains local and fragmented with a large number of players (local developers, companies specialized in biomethane production, oil and gas companies, utilities). Leaders have emerged among these and have built their development locally, such as Archaea Energy in the United States, JMalucelli in Brazil and SGN in the United Kingdom. Acquisition operations have allowed international players in the oil and gas industry and utilities to build up a portfolio of European as well as global assets and projects.

• electricity grids are an integral part of the development of renewable energies, which need to be connected, transported and distributed.

The strategy implemented by the Networks GBU can be summed up in four points:

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

• ensure the operational performance of the Group's gas and electricity networks;

The Group plans to maintain the current level of investment in the green gases division. This approach is largely supported by a rapidly developing regulatory framework supporting the sharp rise in the use of hydrogen and biomethane in the European Union. The gas package adopted in April 2024 sets a European biomethane production target (35 bcm by 2030), and de˱nes low-carbon gases (1) , a regulatory framework for hydrogen infrastructure regulation and infrastructure planning obligations, the implementation of which is entrusted to Member States and operators.

• adapt ENGIE's gas networks to renewable gases (biomethane, hydrogen, e-methane);

• accelerate the production of renewable gases (biomethane, hydrogen, e-methane) in France and in some target countries abroad;

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

• accelerate the development of electricity grids internationally.

Market and competitive environment

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

While the longer-term role of gas (biomethane from different technological procedures, green and blue hydrogen, fossil methane coupled with CO 2 capture and sequestration) in the decarbonization of the French economy remains uncertain, different for each type of consumer and still under discussion within the framework of the National Low-Carbon Strategy ( Stratégie Nationale Bas Carbone – SNBC), replacing gas entirely by electricity is unfeasible both for technical reasons (gas is indispensable for certain industrial processes, and heat pumps cannot be installed in all types of buildings) and economic reasons (excess investments needed in the electricity system if it were unable to provide the ˳exibility provided by the gas system).

In most of the countries in which the Group operates, an independent national regulator establishes a network remuneration system with formulas whose parameters are generally reviewed every four years. There is very little, if any, competition between the various players due to the nature of transmission and distribution assets, and the regulated nature of their markets. In Europe, which is ENGIE's main market, the main network grid managers are EDF, National Grid, Enel and E.ON, with exposure mostly to electricity networks.

section_title: 1.3 DESCRIPTION OF THE GROUP'S ACTIVITIES AT DECEMBER 31, 2025
text:
Presentation of the Group

Description of the Group's activities at December 31, 2025

1.3.2.2 Activities in France

Distribution structures belong to the municipalities even when they are built and ˱nanced by GRDF. As the concession operator, GRDF has exclusive use of these structures. The French Energy Code ( Code de l'Énergie ) recognizes the entitlement of the historical concession operators, i.e., GRDF and 25 local distribution companies, to exclusive service areas. As holders of a “distribution monopoly”, they are the sole operators with which the conceding municipalities may renew the concession.

Apart from the exclusive service areas of GRDF and the local distribution companies, all city authorities not supplied with gas may entrust their public gas distribution to the authorized operator of their choice, following a competitive bidding process.

France's political strategy concerning the energy transition aims to contribute to the carbon neutrality objective (1) by 2050. The priorities of France's climate and energy policy are being updated to re ˳ect the future French Energy-Climate Strategy ( Stratégie Française sur l'Énergie et le Climat – SFEC). The main ˱ndings of the French Energy Regulatory Commission ( Commission de Régulation de l'Energie – CRE) report (1) of April 2023 on the future of gas infrastructure, the conclusions of the public consultation on “decarbonizing the building industry” organized in summer 2023 (highlighting the dif ˱culties associated with a possible ban on the installation of new gas boilers in existing homes), and the public consultation organized in November-December 2024 on the draft 2025-2035 Multi-Annual Energy Plan 3 (PPE3), adopted in February 2026, all demonstrate the importance of gas in a balanced energy mix, which the Group champions.

Regulatory changes

1.3.2.2.1 GRDF

In France, GRDF, an independent subsidiary of ENGIE, develops, operates and maintains distribution networks (201,000 km of networks) and delivers gas for consumers. GRDF is tasked with giving all gas suppliers and biomethane producers equal access to its network. Its new business plan, based on decarbonization, positions the company on a pathway compatible with the Paris Agreement. Its activities are being decarbonized across the three scopes through the transformation of its business lines, a world ˱rst for a gas distribution company. The business plan aims to increase the injection of renewable and low-carbon gases into the networks ˱ve-fold by 2030 and to halve the company's greenhouse gas emissions (1) . It includes support for its stakeholders through their own decarbonization process.

Apart from this speci ˱c case of public service delegations recently awarded after a competitive bidding process, GRDF's activity is remunerated by a tariff set by the French Energy Regulatory Commission (CRE). In July 2024, the CRE approved the ATRD7 tariff, which led to a 27.5% increase compared to the ATRD6 level. This 20-point increase mainly re˳ects the impact of compensation for foregone revenue during the ATRD6 period (due to factors such as Covid, the 2021-2023 energy crisis and high in˳ation), and a faster decline in consumption than forecast when ATRD6 was drawn up. In addition, once a year, within each ATRD tariff period (1) (lasting four years), the CRE decides on any tariff changes to accurately align with the current economic climate and actual consumption. ATRD7 was thus raised by 6.06% on July 1, 2025, re ˳ecting the impact of in˳ation (1.15%), a structural annual growth rate (1.91%), and compensation for tariff revenues generated in 2024 that were lower than forecast.

The tariff enables GRDF to ful˱ll its essential missions in serving local authorities and its residential and industrial customers, the most important of which remains network safety. Over the ATRD7 period, GRDF has the resources it needs to implement its major projects, such as the shift to greener gas and the gas changeover project to convert from B gas to H gas in northern France.

In addition to the major drive to integrate biomethane in the networks, GRDF continues to roll out its Research & Development program to prepare for the inclusion of new renewable gases, with the aim of fully assuming its role in supporting decarbonization and maintaining a balanced, diversi˱ed energy mix.

For the period 2024-2027, CRE has set a compensation rate for GRDF's regulated asset base (RAB) of 4.0% – actual rate before tax – for assets commissioned before 2024, and 5.3% – nominal rate before tax – for investments made from 2024 onwards.

Once a year, the CRE decides on any tariff changes to accurately align with the current economic climate and actual consumption. ATRD7 was thus raised by 6.06% on July 1, 2025, re˳ecting the impact of in˳ation (1.15%), a structural annual growth rate (1.91%) set by the CRE deliberation of February 15, 2024, and compensation for tariff revenues generated in 2024 that were lower than forecast.

The distribution activity has speci ˱c features related to its classi˱cation as a local utility. Each municipality where gas supply is available grants a concession to an authorized distributor to operate the gas distribution utility in its territory. Concessions are entered into or renewed based on a standard agreement established jointly by the French national federation of concession-granting and state-controlled municipalities ( Fédération nationale des collectivités concédantes et régies – FNCCR), the Urban Landowners' Association ( Association foncière urbaine – AFU) and GRDF. The concessiongranting bodies then carry out controls to ensure that the requirements arising from these concession agreements are properly ful ˱lled. In 2022, a new standard concession agreement was adopted by the FNCCR, France Urbaine (the French association for metropolises, urban communities and large cities) and GRDF. This agreement re ˳ects several major changes: in addition to challenges relating to the network's safety and modernization, it focuses on an improved response to territorial challenges to support the local energy transition; clear management and control of investment decisions (investment blueprints and multi-annual investment programs); and the implementation of service quality metrics, with penalties for GRDF in the event of failure to meet commitments. In 2025, around 150 new agreements had been signed with large cities, metropolises and energy syndicates based on this new standard. These long-term agreements – up to 30 years – demonstrate the value recognized by the authorities of the gas network in the energy transition over the long term.

(1) The term is de ˶ned in the glossary, Section 7.9.

section_title: 1.3 DESCRIPTION OF THE GROUP'S ACTIVITIES AT DECEMBER 31, 2025
text:
Presentation of the Group

Description of the Group's activities at December 31, 2025

1.3.2.2.2 NaTran (1)

NaTran is an independent ENGIE subsidiary owned by ENGIE, SIG (Société d’Infrastructures Gazières) and SIG's employees, which have respective stakes in its capital of 60.8%, 38.6% and 0.6%.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

Activities

NaTran is contributing to the growth of hydrogen as an energy carrier by developing hydrogen transport network projects within the fastest growing hydrogen production and consumption basins, including in Moselle-Sarre, Alsace and Fos-sur-Mer. NaTran is also involved in a project to link the Iberian Peninsula to Germany, in particular via its Hy-FEN project between Fos-sur-Mer and Germany, and via an offshore pipeline project linking Barcelona and Fos-sur-Mer undertaken with other partners.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

NaTran is involved in the emergence of carbon capture, use and sequestration for the pipeline logistics part. NaTran is involved in two CO 2 transport projects in France in Dunkirk (onshore pipeline and offshore facility leading to Norway) and Saint-Nazaire and its hinterland.

In addition, the production of biomethane has continued to increase, reaching an injection capacity of 15.5 TWh per year in mid-January 2026 for the networks in France, compared to 14.5 TWh at the end of December 2025.

NaTran operates across most of France, developing, operating and maintaining a gas transmission network comprising more than 32,000 km of buried pipeline and 26 compression stations. The network transmits gas between suppliers, biomethane producers and consumers (distributors or industrial companies directly connected to the transport network). GRTgaz operates its network in a secure and optimized way and provides transport services to network users. It has a public service mandate to guarantee the continuous supply of gas to consumers and facilitate better integration of the European gas markets.

Gas consumption and ˳ows

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

NaTran, and its Elengy subsidiaries, which operate LNG terminals in France, and NaTran Deutschland, which operates the MEGAL transport network in Germany, play a key role on the European gas networks stage.

Regulatory changes

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

In 2025, compared with 2024, gas consumption was down in the industrial sector (excluding centralized electricity production) and buildings (after adjusting for climate effects). Gas consumption for power generation was up, representing a slight rebound on the previous year, where consumption was low due to lower electricity prices (re ˳ecting the relative abundance of nuclear and renewable electricity generation, especially hydroelectric, and low electricity demand in the ˱rst half of 2024). As NaTran's revenues mainly consist of transport capacity sales (2) , the impact of short-term changes in volumes actually consumed in France is minimal.

The methodology and tariffs for the use of transmission networks in France known as “ATRT 8”, applicable for 2024-2027, were set by the CRE on January 30, 2024. This decision also sets the compensation rate for assets integrated into the RAB (2) before December 31, 2023 at 4.1% (actual rate before tax). New assets (integrated into the RAB after that date) will be compensated at the nominal rate of 5.4% before tax, with the term of the regulatory reduction falling from 50 years to 30 years for new pipelines. As a reminder, the compensation rate for NaTran's regulated assets was 4.25% for 2020-2023 (ATRT 7).

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

In 2025, as in 2024 and 2023, the gas transmission activity remained marked by the almost total suspension of Russian gas imports into Europe by pipeline in 2022, which has since led to a major increase in LNG imports to compensate. Flows which previously came from countries to the east of France decreased markedly, or even reversed, with France at times becoming a delivery point for gas heading to the east, notably to Belgium and Germany.

Within this framework, and based on the methodology and in ˳ation assumptions adopted, the CRE deliberation of January 29, 2025 lowered NaTran’s tariffs for use of the natural gas transmission networks, with effect from April 1, 2025, by 0.67% for the main network (2) and 0.55% for the regional network (2) .

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

This change was made possible by NaTran's network, which has been signi ˱cantly enhanced over the past 10 years, and by the streamlining of its use. GRTgaz authorized an increase in the injection of gas from LNG terminals into the network and outbound exports to Germany through the Obergailbach interface point. NaTran has also maintained the Ecogaz system, launched in 2022, to encourage customers to reduce their gas consumption during peak periods if they are able to. All these factors ensured the security of gas supply in France during winter 2024-2025.

1.3.2.2.3 Elengy

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

On June 13, 2024, the European Commission published Directive (EU) 2024/1788 on common rules for the internal markets for renewable gas, natural gas and hydrogen. To support this directive, Regulation (EU) 2024/1789 of June 13, 2024 was published on the internal markets for renewable gas, natural gas and hydrogen. In particular, these documents de ˱ne a framework for regulating access to hydrogen infrastructure, similar to that for natural gas. These provisions will have to be transposed into French law. As a result of this legislation, NaTran intends to position itself as a hydrogen transport network operator.

Green gas projects launched or completed during 2025

NaTran, a player in the energy transition, invests in innovative solutions that favor the development, injection into the networks and use of renewable, low-carbon gas (biomethane and hydrogen), and thus contributes to the achievement of carbon neutrality.

With over 60 years of experience, Elengy is recognized as a major player in the European LNG market. A subsidiary of NaTran since 2017, Elengy owns and operates three LNG terminals in France, located in Montoir-de-Bretagne and Fos‑sur-Mer. These port facilities are designed for receiving lique ˱ed natural gas (LNG), storing it and regasifying it for injection into the transmission network. They had a total regasi˱cation capacity of 21.5 billion m 3 (Gm 3 ) of gas per annum as of December 31, 2025.

section_title: 1.3 DESCRIPTION OF THE GROUP'S ACTIVITIES AT DECEMBER 31, 2025
text:
Presentation of the Group

Description of the Group's activities at December 31, 2025

Elengy’s strategy is structured around three main areas:

• the decarbonization of its assets and activities, by transforming terminals into multi-service hubs for long-term decarbonization;

• the decarbonization of heavy mobility (land and sea);

The 19 th set of sanctions against Russia adopted on October 23, 2025 by the European Union bans short-term contracts for Russian LNG from April 25, 2026, and long-term LNG contracts from January 1, 2027. As the legislation currently stands, these measures will have a very limited impact on Elengy.

The micro-LNG and LNG tanker transshipment and loading services are not regulated.

• the decarbonization of industrial plants, notably through Carbon Capture Use and Storage (CCUE) projects (“GO-CO 2 ” to decarbonize industrial sites in western France and “Rhône CO 2 ” in the Rhône Valley), as well as the Medhyterra project to redevelop part of the Fos Tonkin LNG terminal (1)

1.3.2.2.4 Storengy

into a low-carbon ammonia import terminal.

Installations

With Storengy, the Group is the leader in natural gas underground storage (1) in Europe, with net storage capacity of 12.2 billion m 3 .

Gas storage and conversion to renewable gas

In France , Storengy operates 14 underground storage installations: nine of these are in aquifers (total useful storage volume of 9 billion m 3 ), four are in salt caverns (1 billion m 3 ) and one is in a depleted ˱eld. Two of these sites are in reduced operation according to precise regulatory procedures.

The Montoir-de-Bretagne terminal , commissioned in 1980, is located on the Atlantic coast and receives LNG from various sources. It has a regasi ˱cation capacity of 10 Gm 3 of gas per annum and three tanks with a total capacity of 360,000 m 3 of LNG. The two docks can accommodate tankers transporting up to 267,000 m 3 of LNG, including Q-max tankers (1) . The Montoir terminal has three tanker truck loading bays with an annual capacity of 8,000 loading slots.

After 10 years of reduced operation at the Trois-Fontaine l’Abbaye depleted ˱eld, Storengy has been operating the existing facilities since January 2023 to withdraw some of the gas still present in the reservoir. Revenues from the sale of this gas will contribute to the dismantling or reconversion of the site at the end of its operating period, in around 10 years' time. This activity is part of the overall project to fully rehabilitate the site in consultation with local partners (administration, public bodies, communities, non-pro˱t organizations and residents).

The Fos Cavaou terminal was commissioned in 2010. Its current regasi ˱cation capacity is 10 G m 3 of gas per annum. It has one dock that can accommodate Q-max tankers and three tanks with a total capacity of 330,000 m 3 of LNG. The terminal is also used for reloading LNG tankers and loading trucks for small-scale LNG. Since 2022, Elengy has been developing an LNG loading service for bunker ships enabling cruise ships and container ships to be directly supplied with fuel (some 40 operations were carried out last year). The Fos Cavaou terminal has four tank truck loading bays with an annual capacity of 22,000 loading slots.

In Germany , Storengy Deutschland operates six storage facilities (1.7 billion m 3 ; three salt sites and three depleted sites) and operates a seventh storage facility for a third party.

In the United Kingdom , Storengy UK Ltd operates the storage site in saline caverns in Stublach (400 million m 3 ). With its 20 cavities, this storage facility is currently the largest onshore storage facility in the United Kingdom.

Commissioned in 1972, the Fos Tonkin terminal is located on the Mediterranean coast and receives LNG primarily from Algeria. Its dock can accommodate vessels carrying up to 75,000 m 3 of LNG while its tank has a total capacity of 80,000 m 3 . Its commercial capacity is 1.5 G m 3 . The Fos Tonkin terminal has two tank truck loading bays. LNG reception at the Fos Tonkin terminal will cease at the end of 2028.

In addition to LNG regasi ˱cation, Elengy offers a wide range of complementary services through its facilities:

• LNG carrier reloading;

• transshipment between ships;

• LNG tank truck loading;

• bunker ship loading (for direct supply to cruise ships and container ships).

In Europe , Storengy is preparing to convert storage assets to renewable gas (biomethane, synthetic methane, hydrogen) in order to contribute to decarbonization solutions. In this respect, Storengy ˱nalized the HyPSTER pilot project at Etrez in June 2025, and is developing the GeoH2 project at the Manosque site (conversion of two existing salt caverns for large-scale hydrogen storage). The HyPSTER project is a green hydrogen salt cavern storage demonstrator designed to prove the technical feasibility of gas storage and its ability to provide hydrogen and electricity systems with hourly and seasonal ˳exibility. Other projects are being studied:

Since the end of 2024, Elengy’s Fos Cavaou and Montoir terminals have been certi ˱ed via voluntary schemes recognized under the Renewable Energy Directive (RED) to issue bioLNG Proofs of Sustainability.

• in France , Storgrhyn in the Grand Est region (identifying geological sites with potential for hydrogen storage in salt caverns);

Regulatory changes

• in the United Kingdom , HyKeuper (creation of salt caverns for hydrogen storage as part of the HyNet infrastructure project). Note that HyNet is a cluster including storage, transport and production infrastructures, and downstream hydrogen consumers. The HyKeuper underground hydrogen storage project is an integral part of HyNet;

• in Germany , Salthy (creation of two salt caverns for hydrogen storage).

The LNG terminals are accessible to all LNG suppliers. Access to regasi ˱cation is regulated. The CRE deliberation setting the tariff for the use of regulated LNG terminals (ATTM 7) for the period beginning April 1, 2025 was adopted on February 6, 2025. In particular, it reduces the maximum term for the regulatory reduction to 20 years for new investments at the Fos Cavaou terminal, a period already applicable to the Montoir-de-Bretagne terminal.

section_title: 1.3 DESCRIPTION OF THE GROUP'S ACTIVITIES AT DECEMBER 31, 2025
text:
Presentation of the Group

Description of the Group's activities at December 31, 2025

Regulatory changes

Value chain and strategic role

• Local production : RGE relies on local units to create sustainable energy ecosystems.

• Injection and traceability : introduction of guarantees of origin and certi ˱cation mechanisms to secure the value chain.

Under the Gas Storage Regulation temporarily put in place following the 2022 energy crisis, the EU set a binding gas storage ˱lling target of at least 90% by November 1 of each year. This target was reached at European level every year until November 1, 2024.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

This binding target has exacerbated the dif˱culties of marketing storage capacity in Europe for winter 2025-2026.

• Green mobility and industry : development of bioNGV, a renewable form of NGV (Natural Gas for Vehicles) for road and river transport.

Flagship projects and innovations

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

Faced with this situation, the EU introduced various ˳exibilities when extending the Gas Storage Regulation until 2027, in order to ensure supply security while limiting the impact on gas markets. These measures introduce ˳exibility in terms of time and potentially volume in the event of unfavorable market conditions.

• Advanced anaerobic digestion : integration of technologies enabling the recovery of biogenic CO₂ to produce e-fuels such as e-methane and e-SAF (electro-sustainable aviation fuel).

• Digitalization : monitoring tools to improve unit performance and reduce operating costs, use of arti ˱cial intelligence to optimize input revenue.

Despite unfavorable conditions, Storengy has sold all its available storage capacity for winter 2025-2026 and achieved a ˱ll rate of over 90% before the November 1 deadline, as in previous years since 2022.

Objectives and outlook

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

ENGIE aims for biomethane to represent a signi ˱cant share of its gas portfolio, in line with its ambition for carbon neutrality and its role in the European carbon-free gas backbone. This trajectory is accompanied by investments in R&D to improve yields, reduce costs and develop innovative solutions for mobility and industry.

In the context of the energy transition, gas storage plays a dual role in providing security and ˳exibility to the energy system in an environment where gas ˳ows are more unpredictable. LNG, which is more subject to global market dynamics, accounts for a growing share of supply. On the other hand, demand is more variable, in particular due to the growing share of renewables in the energy mix. Storage infrastructures are therefore essential to balance these effects.

1.3.2.2.6 Hydrogen activities

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

Purpose and Strategy

Hydrogen is a key transition energy vector, and ENGIE aims to develop strong positions throughout the entire value chain of hydrogen production, networks, mobility and trading.

More speci˱cally on the revenue model, the decision of the Energy Regulatory Commission (CRE) on January 31, 2024 sets the terms and conditions of the ATS3 tariff for Storengy France for the period 2024-2027. The compensation rate for assets integrated into the regulated asset base (RAB) before December 31, 2023 is 4.6% real before tax. In addition, new assets (integrated into the RAB after that date) will be compensated by a nominal rate of 5.9% before tax, over a period of 30 years rather than 50 years.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

1.3.2.2.5 Renewable Gas

In Europe , the Group bene ˱ts from its portfolio of industrial and local authority customers (Local Energy Infrastructures GBU) as well as signi˱cant renewable energy production capacity and the commercial know-how of the Supply & Energy Management GBU.

In France , Germany and the United Kingdom , the Group is expanding around the existing transport networks (NaTran – see Section 1.3.2.2.2) and storage networks (Storengy – see Section 1.3.2.2.4) that are a central part of the future European hydrogen backbone.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

The Group prioritizes developing projects in countries where renewable hydrogen can be produced competitively and where it has a strong position, in particular those where public policies encourage hydrogen development, with the aim of supporting its customers’ energy transition.

Description of activities

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

The Networks GBU coordinates all of the Group's hydrogen activities, which are developed in the various GBU according to their relevant expertise.

Renewable Gas (RG), a major player in the production of green gas, is the ENGIE entity dedicated to the development and production of biomethane in Europe. With 350 employees and 42 production units in four European countries – France , the United Kingdom , Belgium and the Netherlands – RG had a total installed capacity of 1.2 TWh/year at the end of 2025. RG is engaged in development activities in Poland and Spain , but has no units in operation. More generally, RG is continuing its development in Europe while accelerating industrialization and increasing the capacity of its units, with the aim of producing 10 TWh by 2035. Biomethane, produced through anaerobic digestion of organic matter (agricultural ef ˳uents, biowaste, etc.), is injected into existing gas networks and provides an immediate solution for replacing natural gas. ENGIE is playing an active role in this shift to greener alternatives by developing partnerships with the farming community, recycling waste and contributing to the circular economy.

Regulatory changes

Large-scale production of decarbonized hydrogen : ENGIE has a comprehensive and phased approach, developing projects with its industrial customers in the most favorable geographic areas. ENGIE is targeting industries that would otherwise be dif ˱cult to decarbonize, as well as existing hydrogen consumers. In sectors where electri˱cation is not always possible or ˱nancially viable, hydrogen may be a solution. This is the case in particular for the steel industry, re˱ning (conventional or biofuel), and the production of e-molecules (ammonia, methanol, synthetic kerosene, etc.). ENGIE aims to reach 4 GW of electrolysis capacity by 2035.

As part of its goal of achieving carbon neutrality, the EU is seeking to develop the production of renewable and low-carbon hydrogen on a large scale through its REPowerEU plan. Binding targets for the consumption of renewable hydrogen and hydrogen derivatives have been set for industry and transport under the EU RED III directive. The ReFuelEU aviation regulation also sets binding targets for e-fuels. These are positive changes that demonstrate a strengthened political drive but that still need to be implemented in practice, particularly through a simpli ˱ed and accelerated funding process.

section_title: 1.3 DESCRIPTION OF THE GROUP'S ACTIVITIES AT DECEMBER 31, 2025
text:
Presentation of the Group

Description of the Group's activities at December 31, 2025

Networks: The adaptation and conversion of networks for development of hydrogen is a priority for the Group.

In July 2025, ENGIE commenced the HyCoFlex project to inject 100% hydrogen into a Siemens 12 MW gas turbine, following the Hy ˳exPower project, paving the way for the use of hydrogen in its gas-˱red power plants in Europe. By testing several mixtures of hydrogen and methane, the project makes it possible to concretely measure the impact of hydrogen on turbine performance and maintenance.

In addition to projects connecting hydrogen producers and consumers within industrial hubs, NaTran is heavily involved in the development of a European hydrogen backbone through the H2med project, a hydrogen pipeline linking Portugal and Spain to France and Germany (see Section 1.3.2.2.2), for which pre-feasibility studies are ongoing. Regulatory changes

In Peru , throughout 2025, the Ministry of Energy and Mines continued to develop regulations concerning vertical integration in the electricity sector with a view to clarifying the rules separating electricity production, transmission and distribution activities. This clari ˱cation will give ENGIE greater regulatory certainty to pursue its expansion in the electricity transmission segment.

Furthermore, in September 2025, a new law on the promotion of private investment through public-private partnerships (PPP) was enacted, establishing the regulatory framework within which the Private Investment Promotion Agency, ProInversión, organizes tenders and shortening the timeframes for launching these tenders for remunerated electricity transmission infrastructure projects. The implementing regulations for this law were published in December 2025.

The Ten-Year Energy Expansion Plan (PDE) in Brazil outlines the energy sector’s expansion prospects over a 10-year horizon, and is updated annually. The PDE is built around three key aspects of energy planning: economic (meeting energy needs linked to economic expansion), socioenvironmental (ensuring access to energy for the entire population, promoting regional integration and taking into account other socio-environmental aspects) and strategic (optimizing the use of energy resources with a mediumand long-term vision). In the 2025-2034 PDE reference scenario, some 30,000 km of new transmission lines are planned to be added to the grid by December 2034, bringing the total highvoltage capacity of the Brazilian power system to 218,000 km. For substations, an additional 82,000 MVA (megavoltamperes) of installed capacity is planned, to reach a total of 564,000 MVA by 2034.

Finally, in September 2025, the Andean Community accepted the Republic of Chile’s request to adhere to the regulatory framework for the interconnection of sub-regional transmission networks, marking the ˱rst of˱cial step towards the establishment of an electricity transmission interconnection between Chile and Peru, and opening up new development prospects for ENGIE.

In Chile , following a legislative amendment at the end of 2024, responsibility for issuing calls for tenders for public utility reinforcement work now lies with the asset owner. In this new regulatory context, in September 2025 ENGIE organized the ˱rst public tender to select an EPC (Engineering, Procurement & Construction) contractor to carry out reinforcement work at the Roncacho site, in line with the needs identi˱ed in the annual transmission system extension report.

With nearly 28,500 employees, it meets the needs of local authorities, industry and the service sector, with a shared ambition: to accelerate decarbonization in regions through three key business lines – district heating and cooling networks, energy production on industrial or tertiary sites, and energy performance services.

S&EM's strategy to develop its green energy portfolio is supported by cultural change initiatives and speci˱c training programs, as well as the inclusion of social, environmental and carbon emissions criteria in the decision-making process. By proactively reducing the carbon intensity of its sales, S&EM contributes to the Group's climate goals.

1.3.4.2 Activities of S&EM

S&EM activities are divided into three main areas of expertise.

Asset optimization

In 2025, S&EM optimized nearly 60 GW of energy assets for the Group and its customers:

Regarding electricity assets , S&EM provides marketing and dispatching activities for ENGIE's production assets as well as for third-party assets.

Concerning gas asset management , S&EM:

• manages the upstream supply, transmission and storage capacities, including recovery and optimization of ˳exibility (combined cycle gas power plants) through the markets;

• optimizes a portfolio of LNG, biomethane and biomass assets.

Supplying energy and services to BtoB and BtoC customers

ENGIE engages in BtoB supply activities in 12 countries: serving more than 200,000 business customers, including major international accounts and around 800 global customers, S&EM develops renewable electricity supply activities (renewable power purchase agreements – PPAs) and offers customized solutions to help BtoB customers achieve their environmental, social and governance objectives. These solutions cover green energy supply, guarantees of origin, energy traceability, carbon offsetting mechanisms, energy ef ˱ciency and integrated offerings combining supply, risk management and carbon performance management. BtoB sales momentum is based on growth in renewable electricity sales, support for customers’ decarbonization pathways, and the strengthening of long-term partnerships in the face of volatile energy markets. ENGIE is also developing 24/7 decarbonized energy supply offers, aimed at ensuring that every hour of its customers’ consumption is covered by decarbonized production, making power reliable as well as sustainable.

Risk management

S&EM ensures security of supply for the Group’s customers, supplying them with natural gas, green and low-carbon gas (biomethane, hydrogen) and electricity. It serves residential, business and large industrial customers as well as other ENGIE commercial entities.

S&EM manages the risks of the Group's physical and ˱nancial energy portfolio through an integrated approach combining market expertise, bespoke hedging strategies and direct access to energy markets. This risk management covers the entire value chain, from procurement to supply for BtoB and BtoC customers.

ENGIE engages in BtoC supply activities in six countries: France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Romania, Italy and Australia. It manages around 20 million BtoC contracts for electricity, gas and related energy services. These activities rely on close proximity to local markets and the ability to serve large customer portfolios, particularly in France and Belgium, which account for a signi ˱cant proportion of sales volumes.

Its teams draw on their in-depth knowledge of electricity and gas markets, production assets and customer consumption pro˱les to ensure reliable supply. Hedging strategies are tailored to customer portfolios and time horizons, incorporating price, volume and imbalance risks.

Faced with the growing complexity of the energy market, ENGIE’s ambition is to embody the image of a trusted partner to its customers by developing offers tailored to their needs, and to help them choose the best deal while reducing their carbon footprint. BtoC sales momentum is notably driven by enriching offers, digitalizing the customer experience and developing services to help customers consume less, better and at the right time. In 2025, ENGIE also launched a strategy to refocus its BtoC activities on energy supply.

On February 21, 2025, the European Commission approved under EU state aid rules the agreement between ENGIE and the Belgian government.

The entity's sites in Belgium are located in Doel, Tihange and Brussels. Electrabel operates the Doel and the Tihange nuclear power plants in compliance with the strictest nuclear safety standards. The Doel 3 (1,006 MW) and Tihange 2 (1,008 MW) plants were permanently shut down on September 23, 2022 and January 31, 2023, respectively. Following the de ˱nitive shutdown of Doel 1 (445 MW) on February 14, 2025, Tihange 1 (962 MW) on September 30, 2025 and Doel 2 (445 MW) on November 30, 2025, the remaining power plants in operation at the end of 2025 (Doel 4 and Tihange 3) represent a total installed capacity in Belgium of 2056 MW (of which 210 MW belong to the EDF group and 1,846 MW to a 50/50 partnership between the Belgian government and ENGIE). The Group also has 1,118 MW of drawing rights in the Tricastin and Chooz B power plants in France.

The transaction was completed on March 14, 2025, and Doel 4 and Tihange 3 were restarted well before November 1, 2025. The Group paid the amount of €15 billion 2022 in two installments according to waste categories of which €12.2 billion upon closing in March 2025 and the balance of €3.6 billion following the restart of the Doel 4 power plant on October 14 (see Note 17.2 of Section 6.2.2 Notes to the consolidated ˱nancial statements).

The initial legal framework provided for the gradual withdrawal from the operation of nuclear power plants in Belgium between 2022 and 2025. Following a decision dated March 18, 2022, the Belgian government decided to take the necessary measures to extend the operating life of Doel 4 and Tihange 3 by 10 years.

Under the Phoenix agreements, Electrabel sold to its parent company (i) International Power (international activities) and (ii) Engie Invest International (internal ˱nancial vehicles), thus limiting the restrictions on capital transactions imposed by the Belgian Commission for Nuclear Provisions (CPN) to operating activities in Europe.

On December 13, 2023, ENGIE and the Belgian government signed the ˱nal agreement on the extension of the Tihange 3 and Doel 4 nuclear reactors and all obligations related to nuclear waste. It stipulates:

• the commitment of the two parties to carry out a ˳exible long-term operation arrangement for an estimated investment amount of between €1.6 billion and €2 billion, and to make their best efforts to restart the Doel 4 and Tihange 3 nuclear units from November 2025;

The Group assumes obligations resulting from the Belgian Act of April 11, 2003 as amended by the Act dated July 12, 2022, relating to the provisions made for the dismantling of nuclear power plants and for the management of spent nuclear fuel. The Act of July 12, 2022 provides in particular for the full ˱nancing of nuclear provisions by 2030 and a strengthening of the control of the Belgian Commission for Nuclear Provisions on certain decisions relating to the capital of Electrabel and to Synatom.

• the establishment of a legal structure dedicated to the two extended nuclear units, equally owned by the Belgian State and ENGIE;

In the framework of the above-mentioned ˱nal agreement, the Act of July 12, 2022 will be amended to take into account the establishment of a lump sum payment for future costs related to the treatment of nuclear waste (€15 billion 2022 ), with Electrabel remaining exclusively responsible only for dismantling obligations (and still subject to nuclear provisions). The three-yearly review due in 2025 was sent to the CPN on October 2.

• the business model for the extension with a balanced distribution of risks, in particular through a Contract for Difference mechanism for compensation of electricity production. The strike price will be based on the actual cost of extending the nuclear units. This cost is not yet known but will be estimated based on nuclear safety requirements established by the Federal Agency for Nuclear Control (AFCN). An initial price ˱xed at end-2025 will be updated in 2028 based on the known amount of the ˱nal cost of the extension, to cover the period up to 2035;
