2.1 RISK MANAGEMENT PROCESS

2.1.1 Enterprise risk management policy

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

Risk analysis and coordination of action plans are performed in collaboration with all the Group's divisions and are subject to an additional review alongside the Group's four Global Business Units (GBU).

The Group has adopted an Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) policy, the principles of which are consistent with professional standards (including ISO (1) 31000 and the Federation of European Risk Management Associations). The policy sets out ENGIE's ambition to “manage its risks in order to ensure its performance”.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

The Group's Enterprise Risk Management Policy applies to the Group's businesses and controlled entities, while observing the governance rules that apply to each entity.

Each year, the Group's ERM process begins with a prior-year risk review by the Executive Committee. An ERM campaign is then launched across the Group, setting out guidelines for risk management throughout the year. It results in a new Group risk review that is presented to the Executive Committee, and then to the Audit Committee. After examining the review, the Audit Committee gives its opinion on the effectiveness of the risk management framework to the Board of Directors.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

This policy promotes risk-taking at a reasonable level from a legal perspective, which is acceptable to generally held public opinion and economically viable. It stipulates that all managers are Risk Managers. Generally, the Management Committees of Group entities are the main bodies that determine the actions to be taken to manage risks, except when a speci ˱c risk committee is created, such as for energy market risk or ethical risk.

The acknowledgment of risks reported by the operating entities and functional departments is supplemented by interviews with managers, an analysis of publications by external analysts and a review of major events (see Section 3.1.1.5 Risk management process and internal control of the Sustainability Statement).

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

The Head of Risk Management and Insurance is responsible for ensuring the effectiveness of the risk management framework. He/she coordinates the designated Chief Risk Of˱cers of each of the operating entities and Corporate Functions. These Chief Risk Of˱cers assess the entity or Function's overall risk exposure and ensure that risk mitigation plans are implemented.

2.1.2 Crisis management

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

As part of a continuous improvement process, each Group entity carries out at least one crisis drill per year across an appropriate scope that meets regulatory requirements. Speci˱c training is also available to internal stakeholders involved in crisis management.

The ENGIE Group has structured a global crisis management system, built to respond to the occurrence of all types of exceptional situations that could affect its operations, employees, customers and partners. This system, deployed at each level of the Group, guarantees that an effective warning system is in place, along with a major incident escalation process.

The level of maturity of the system is assessed annually through a structured self-assessment based on an internal control framework. Peer reviews are carried out on a panel of entities to con˱rm the assessments and share best practices.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

A consolidated annual report is presented to the Group's management, summarizing the lessons learned from events, drills and assessments, and identifying the improvement actions to be taken in coordination with all entities.

When a critical event occurs, an analysis of the situation is carried out by a local duty of ˱cer who may, when necessary, set up a locally run crisis unit and inform the senior duty of˱cer. Crisis units can also be set up at a higher level to provide operational or methodological support to the entity concerned, or to ensure the strategic decision-making necessary for the overall management of the situation. Decisions are made at the most appropriate level of the organization, according to the principle of subsidiarity, to ensure swift, consistent and effective action.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

Despite the robustness of this system, it cannot eliminate the possibility of a crisis disrupting the Group's activities and operations. Similarly, it does not guarantee the absence of any impacts on the Group or its external stakeholders.

To ensure that critical activities are not disrupted and that operations can be rapidly restored, business and information systems continuity and recovery plans are drawn up and updated for the crisis scenarios deemed a priority by the Group and its entities.

With regard to the Brazilian gas market, whose legislation is currently being harmonized between countries with a view to opening it up, the main risk for ENGIE's gas transmission subsidiary (TAG) relates to the planned transport system “bypass” project (direct connection of energy sources to local energy distributors or to end-consumers). Criticality: Risk trend: Decrease

In Belgium, Electrabel, a Group subsidiary, partly owns and fully operates seven pressurized water reactors at two nuclear power plants at Doel and Tihange. Five reactors in this ˳eet were permanently shut down: Doel 3 and Tihange 2 on September 23, 2022 and January 31, 2023; Doel 1 and Doel 2 on February 14, 2025 and November 30, 2025; and Tihange 1 on September 30, 2025. The Tihange 3 and Doel 4 units have been extended by 10 years within BE-Nucléaire, a joint venture equally owned with the Belgian state.

Electrabel established governance principles for the operation, maintenance and dismantling of nuclear power plants based on its experience as an operator. It is also active in employee recruitment, training and retention, both for facilities in operation and nuclear services entities, and is involved in developing new services. These activities are subject to several kinds of risks, at regulatory and political level, in operational terms for the operation, maintenance and dismantling of power plants and at the ˱nancial level.

For the residual risks that the Group must manage:

Costs associated with the dismantling of facilities and the management of nuclear waste and spent fuel are included in the costs of nuclear electricity generation and are the subject of provisions in this regard. Securing nuclear provisions

The agreement with the Belgian Government in December 2023 (payment in full of a lump sum discharge amount of €15 billion 2022 for future costs related to waste treatment) has considerably reduced the risk inherent to the cost of waste management, which has been de ˱nitively ˱xed with no residual liability for the operator once the waste has been packaged in accordance with the Contractual Transfer Criteria (CTC) de˱ned with the National Agency for Radioactive Waste and Enriched Fissile Material ( Organisme National des Déchets Radioactifs et des Matières Fissiles Enrichies – ONDRAF) and established by Royal Decree.

The nuclear operator is responsible only for the risks related to:

The ˱nancial risk associated with securing nuclear provisions was considerably reduced following the ˱nal payments to Hedera of €11.5 billion 2022 in March 2025 for the transfer of category B and C waste, and €3.5 billion 2022 when the units were restarted in October 2025 for the transfer of category A waste.

• the cost of dismantling power plants and the cost of managing on-site storage of spent fuel waste until completion of dismantling operations and until 2050 at the latest; these costs are subject to triennial review;

• compliance of the volumetric credit of radioactive waste and with the conditioning of waste in accordance with the CTC and the ful ˱lment of its commitments.

Securing nuclear provisions

For the balance of secured nuclear provisions, management of the investments is entrusted to a team led by a chief investment of ˱cer within Synatom. An investment committee composed of experts, who are all Synatom directors, is responsible for overseeing investment decisions. To this end, the investment policy is based on a controlled risk pro˱le aimed at achieving performance objectives and substantial diversi˱cation of risks, and is based on a rigorous risk control policy.

Securing nuclear provisions creates ˱nancial risks speci˱c to nuclear activities.

This mainly concerns the risk of return on invested ˱nancial assets, which are the counterparty to the provisions set aside within Synatom (an Electrabel subsidiary), under the supervision of the Commission for Nuclear Provisions ( Commission des Provisions Nucléaire – CPN). At December 31, 2025, these dedicated ˱nancial assets are invested to the tune of €5.6 billion in SICAV funds and will represent the whole of the nuclear provisions by 2031 (see Note 17.2.4 of Section 6.2.2 Notes to the consolidated ˱nancial statements). The volatility of the value of ˱nancial assets representing consideration for nuclear provisions represents a signi˱cant risk for the Group.

2.3 INTERNAL CONTROL PROCEDURES

2.3.1 Internal control objectives

2.3.1.1 Legal framework of application

ENGIE's internal control complies with the Financial Security Act adopted on August 1, 2003; and is based on the COSO II model of the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission and the French Financial Markets Authority

(Autorité des marchés ˱nanciers - AMF) reference framework. It is guided by a Group policy which sets out, with regard to the applicable regulatory framework, the expectations and objectives of the Internal Control function.

2.3.1.2 Internal control objectives

The purpose of ENGIE's internal control function is to provide reasonable assurance (as described by the COSO) that its activities are subject to adequate controls in terms of the following objectives:

Consequently, ENGIE's internal control system is constantly adapted to take into account the challenges facing the Group. These adaptations respond to constant changes in regulations, the transformation of the organization, the development of new business lines or digital technology.

• appropriate implementation and optimization of operations;

• the reliability of ˱nancial information; and

• compliance with laws and regulations as well as with instructions and guidelines set by Executive Management.

The internal control process applies to Group subsidiaries according to a ˱nancial materiality threshold. However, companies accounted for by the equity method may choose to adopt a different internal control system, the effectiveness of which they report to their governance bodies. In 2025, ˱ve subsidiaries above the threshold were concerned.

• directly and indirectly overseeing the actions of the Internal Control function within the Group; and

Internal control is ˱rst and foremost a managerial responsibility that applies at all levels within the Group so that each manager, as the “˱rst line of defense,” is responsible for developing an appropriate internal control system and for overseeing its ef˱ciency.

• managing and coordinating the system as a stakeholder of the “second line of defense” with the other functions (see Section 2.3.2.3.3). Each one is responsible for the suitability and effectiveness of its internal control system in its respective area.

The internal control function is composed of all these elements.

The second line of defense in the internal control system is the responsibility of each functional department. 3.1.1 General information [ESRS 2]

3.1.1.1 Methodological note

3.1.1.1.1 General basis for preparation of the Sustainability Statement [BP-1]

Basis for preparation [BP-1 5a, b]

• due to the complexity of European sustainability reporting regulations (including the Taxonomy) and the absence of a single, consensus-based interpretation of the texts, the Group has retained its reporting principles established in 2024, particularly with regard to the de ˱nition of operational control. For the ENGIE Group this is based on the analysis of ˱nancial control, before adding some speci˱c analysis criteria for operational control;

This Sustainability Statement has been prepared in accordance with the Directive of December 14, 2022 amending Regulation no. 537/2014, Directive no. 2004/109/EC, Directive no. 2006/ 43/EC and the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) no. 2013/34/EU. These directives were transposed in France by transposition order no. 2023-1142 of December 6, 2023, amended by Law No. 2025-391 of April 30, 2025 and supplemented by Delegated Regulation no. 2023/2772 of July 31, 2023. The latter establishes the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS). This Sustainability Statement has also been prepared in accordance with the European Taxonomy set out in Article 8 of Regulation 2020/852.

• the ENGIE Group has opted to apply as of the end of 2025 the provisions of the “Omnibus” Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/73, which introduced measures simplifying the generic Do No Signi ˱cant Harm (DNSH) criteria regarding pollution prevention and reduction, as well as the models for reporting results. For 2025, the Group did not consider the option offered by the Delegated Regulation of applying a materiality approach to assessing the eligibility and alignment of its economic activities. However, this possibility will be examined for the 2026 ˱nancial year;

This Sustainability Statement is based on a double materiality assessment (described in more detail below), which identi ˱es the Environmental, Social or Governance (ESG) matters on which ENGIE has a material (positive or negative) impact and those that have a major effect on the Group’s ˱nancial performance (risks or opportunities).

• lastly, the internal control process is currently being adapted to the new requirements of the standards. Signi ˱cant progress has been achieved since last year, and these efforts will continue in future years (see Section 3.1.1.5).

Scope of consolidation

This information was prepared in an evolving context characterized by uncertainties regarding the interpretation of the texts, the absence of established practices – particularly for double materiality assessments – and the updating of the internal control system. In this regulatory environment, which remains uncertain at the beginning of 2026, ENGIE has chosen to maintain a level of disclosure similar to last year’s. Consequently, the work carried out this year is a continuation of that undertaken in the previous year.

Several points are worth highlighting:

In accordance with ESRS standards, the Sustainability Statement applies the same scope as the ˱nancial statements. This means that the ESG reporting scope for own operations is consistent with the scope of consolidation of the ˱nancial statements covering both the parent company and its (fully consolidated) subsidiaries. Joint operations are also considered as ENGIE’s own operations, up to the amount of their share in the capital.

• the double materiality assessment is identical to that performed in 2024, as no signi ˱cant events were identi˱ed whose impact on the ENGIE Group’s structure or business model would have altered the results of the assessment or the resulting disclosure requirements;

Associates (i.e., those over which ENGIE exercises signi˱cant in˳uence) and joint ventures (i.e., those over which ENGIE exercises joint control) are accounted for using the equity method and are included in the upstream or downstream segments of the value chain (VC) in proportion to their percentage holding. Financial assets (loans, equity and debt investments) are considered as “business relationships” and if they are material, may give rise to value chain information.

• certain quantitative information relies on the judgment and estimates of the ENGIE Group’s Executive Management and may involve uncertainties, particularly in the case of longterm forecasts, as explained in Section 3.1.1.1.2. These uncertainties, judgments and estimates are set out for the main metrics concerned in the Sustainability Statement;

The basis for the preparation and calculation of the metrics follows the above principles, with the exception of certain speci ˱c metrics which require a broader scope of application. For these metrics, the methodology applied is speci˱ed in the sections dealing with the relevant ESRS.

• as speci ˱ed in the paragraph “Methodology used to calculate the Group's total GHG emissions” in part of Section 3.1.2.1.6 Climate metrics [E1-5, E1-6], CO 2 emissions related to waste gas recovery services for a steel-producing customer are excluded from the Group's Scope 1;

• in accordance with its commitments, the Group is reporting certain data points this year that were unavailable in 2024. However, some data points remain to be reported or completed in future years. These notably include:

[BP-1 5c] As with the ˱rst year of reporting and with the exception of the double materiality assessment and exceptions speci˱ed in the relevant section where applicable, the value chain includes tier 1 suppliers and tier 1 consumers and end‑users – i.e., direct residential customers who purchase the company’s products and services for personal use.

• the disclosure of metrics related to water and soil pollutants and supplier payment terms, and information on ˱nes, penalties and compensation for damages as a result of human rights incidents,

• alignment of calculation methodologies with ESRS for certain compensation metrics;

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

The GBU operates in two geographic areas: Europe, with ˱ve priority countries (France, Germany, Italy, Spain and Poland), and Asia & Middle East.

The GBU sources its supplies from industrial groups that manufacture or install energy network equipment or provide digital services.

The Renewable & Flex Power GBU develops, builds, ˱nances, operates and maintains renewable power generation, power storage and ˳exible thermal assets. It focuses mainly on six technologies: hydroelectricity, solar power, onshore wind power, offshore wind power, battery storage collocated with a renewable asset and combined cycle gas turbines (CCGT). It operates in four geographic areas: Europe, North America, South America and the AMEA region (Asia, the Middle East and Africa).

Its main customers include cities, local authorities, industrial companies, the service sector and collective housing.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

The Supply & Energy Management (S&EM) GBU optimizes the operation of ENGIE’s energy assets and ensures reliable, sustainable energy supply for customers. Its main activities cover three ˱elds:

Most of the future investments of the Renewables GBU will be focused on the ˱ve priority markets – namely France, Brazil, Chile, the United States and offshore wind. There will be increased ambition in the AMEA region (Asia, Middle East and Africa), particularly in India and South Africa.

Asset optimization : S&EM optimizes energy assets (electricity, gas, LNG, biomethane, biomass) by managing market access, dispatching, procurement, transport, storage and the monetization of asset ˳exibility.

The Renewable & Flex Power GBU’s supply chain consists of renewable energy production equipment suppliers and installers, as well as thermal equipment suppliers for constructing and maintaining its facilities.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

The GBU’s main customers are local authorities, industries, businesses and residential customers who own the land on which the installations are located.

Energy and service supply : S&EM guarantees the security of the supply of natural gas, green gas and low-carbon gas (e.g., biomethane and hydrogen), and electricity for a diverse customer base.

Risk management : S&EM manages the risks associated with physical and ˱nancial energy portfolios through hedging strategies and market expertise.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

The Networks GBU is responsible for developing, operating and maintaining gas networks (distribution and transport networks, storage and LNG terminals) and electricity networks, as well as the production of biomethane and hydrogen, in France and target countries.

The GBU operates worldwide, speci˱cally in six countries: France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Romania, Italy and Australia for B2C supply and in 12 countries for B2B supply.

Its main customers are:

• other Group entities;

The four LNG terminals are located in France and Chile. Storage sites are located in France, Germany, Romania and the United Kingdom. Transport is provided in France, Brazil and Mexico. Distribution to residential customers is provided in Europe and Mexico.

• energy consumers (industries and businesses);

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

• distributors and resellers in the energy sector;

• trading companies and investment funds;

• residential customers and small businesses.

The Networks GBU’s strategy is to ensure the operational performance of infrastructure, adapt it for renewable gases and accelerate the production of biomethane and, more broadly, low-carbon gases in France and several targeted international countries, as well as to develop international power grids.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

GBU obtains its energy supplies from energy trading platforms, the Group’s energy assets and from a number of historical gas suppliers, notably in Norway, Algeria, Middle East and the United States.

The Networks GBU sources its supplies from major industrial companies that manufacture and install pipes, gas compression, treatment and metering stations, biogas production and injection (1) installations, and electricity pylons and networks.

Its customers are the shippers who transport their gas or electricity, and the end-consumers who connect to the distribution or transport networks.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

The Nuclear operating entity is dedicated to the operational management of the two nuclear reactors in Belgium and the rights held by EDF’s two power plants in France. The initial legal framework provided for the gradual withdrawal from the operation of nuclear power plants in Belgium between 2022 and 2025. Following a decision dated March 18, 2022, the Belgian government decided to take the necessary measures to extend the operating life of two reactors, Doel 4 and Tihange 3, by 10 years, until 2035.

This activity sources its uranium mainly from a major player in the sector, and from industrial groups specializing in nuclear equipment.

This activity supplies electricity to Electrabel customers and on the wholesale electricity market.

The Other-Tractebel business provides engineering and consulting services to private and public sector customers in 40 countries, offering integrated solutions in the ˱elds of energy, water and infrastructure.

The Local Energy Infrastructures GBU supports its customers in decarbonizing and managing their energy consumption. The solutions proposed are divided into three categories: local energy networks, on-site energy production, and energy management and performance services. Local energy networks produce and deliver ˱nal energy (heating, steam, cooling, electricity) to several users by optimizing the use of green energies available in the area (biomass, geothermal, thermal solar, etc.), while developing highly energy-ef˱cient technologies. On-site energy production depends on networks that produce on a site-wide scale (industrial or service sites) via lowcarbon utilities of the ˱nal energy required for its operation (heating, cooling, electricity, steam, compressed air, etc.). The GBU develops, modernizes and operates these networks. It offers customers contracts with commitments to reduce the energy consumption and associated CO 2 emissions of their

ENGIE’s engagement with its stakeholders at the operational level is based on several tools:

The Stakeholder Committee, which each year brings together several members of civil society to discuss the Group’s strategic choices and projects, organized a meeting on January 27, 2025 in the presence of the Chairman of the Board of Directors and the Chief Executive Of ˱cer. The discussion provided an opportunity to share the results of the double materiality assessment and collect feedback from participants which will be taken into account during the next double materiality exercise.

• a toolbox made available to entities, which structures the stakeholder engagement process in six stages: context analysis, mapping of stakeholders, identi ˱cation of their relevant matters, development of an action plan, monitoring and evaluation of its impact;

• an in-house training program run by ENGIE University, aimed primarily at project managers and business developers.

[SBM-2 45b] At the end of 2023, the double materiality assessment helped to gather the main stakeholders’ interests and views on the environmental, social and governance matters related to the Group’s activities. These consultations led to a broad convergence of views on the prioritization of environmental and social matters, with the prioritization resulting from the work on quantifying social and environmental impacts.

After drawing up a list of potentially material IROs, ENGIE determined their materiality in two stages: their rating and then the determination of a materiality threshold.

• “General information on the methodology chosen” workshop;

To assess the materiality of the impact and ˱nancial materiality, the main parameters below have been evaluated on a scale of 0 to 3, based essentially on qualitative factors:

• “Climate and circular economy” workshop;

• “Biodiversity, pollution and water” workshop;

• “Social and personal labor” workshop;

• for the materiality of the impact: the scale and the scope for actual impacts, the irremediable character of the impact for actual negative impacts, and the likelihood of the impact for potential impacts. In the case of a potential negative impact, the severity of the impact takes precedence over its likelihood. This approach has been extended to all potential negative impacts, in addition to those affecting human rights. ENGIE has therefore chosen to raise the probability levels of these impacts from very rare to certain, to avoid probability that is too low, thus diminishing the severity of an impact;

These workshops, which brought together all the Group’s business units and geographies based on their business and their expertise in the matters identi ˱ed, made it possible to identify and consolidate an initial list of potentially material IROs. All GBU were represented in these workshops in order to take account of any speci˱cities existing in certain businesses or activities.

• for ˱nancial materiality: the current and future effects on the Company’s ˱nancial performance, by considering the likelihood of impact and the potential scale in parallel.

These IROs may concern ENGIE’s own activities and/or those of upstream or downstream stakeholders in its value chain.

Solar generation The impact of climate change is calculated by taking into account changes in solar irradiation and temperature, which affect module performance.

Wind generation The impact of climate change is calculated using power curves (depending on turbine type/model) that relate wind speed to available power.

The effects of temperature are accounted for either by shutdown in the event of high temperatures or by a gradual decrease in production.

Demand for heating and cooling is calculated based on heating and cooling degree days, population density, and assumptions about commercial and residential buildings. Domestic hot water demand is also included.

The analysis uses CMIP5 or CMIP6 (1) global models or CORDEX (2) regional models, as appropriate, all of which use IPCC scenarios as input data. Wherever possible, ENGIE uses bias-corrected data with respect to recent climate, in line with the IPCC’s work on the impacts of climate change. The use of bias-corrected data is crucial for anything that involves thresholds or absolute values. For example, in the case of wind power, ENGIE uses power curves that are highly dependent on these adjustments.

[ESRS 2 IRO-1 21, AR 13a, AR 13b] With regard to transition risks and opportunities related to climate change, the Group annually updates various energy scenarios including an Energy Transition scenario for Europe (15 countries) to 2050, in order to address current and future challenges and adapt its business model. The chosen projection horizon (2050) covers ENGIE’s entire decarbonization pathway (Net Zero 2045), as well as the systems in which the Group operates (e.g., goal of contributing to carbon neutrality in Europe by 2050).

(1) CMIP6 (or 5) is the 6 th (or 5 th ) phase of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project, a global collaborative project of climate modelers whose work is a reference in terms of climate science models. The scenarios are determined by the Group using internal forecasting models and are based on the following speci ˱c elements of the downstream value chain:

• forward market prices over the liquidity period for fuel, CO 2 and electricity in each market against a backdrop of volatile energy prices;

[ESRS 2 IRO-1 AR 13b] ENGIE’s Net Zero scenario highlights the need to combine all renewable energy sources to ensure the resilience of the energy system and the competitiveness of European economies. Given the signi ˱cant interconnection of energy systems across Europe, the decarbonization pathway models integrate 15 European countries. ENGIE’s scenario uses the most relevant existing decarbonization levers, while leaving room for emerging technologies.

• beyond this period, mediumand long-term energy prices were determined by the Group based on macroeconomic assumptions and fundamental supply and demand equilibrium models (electricity demand, development of installed capacity, etc.), as well as mediumand long-term forecasts of fuel and CO 2 prices.

The scenarios are updated annually, and a central scenario is then used for medium-and long-term commodity projections, notably for gas and electricity, ˱nancial projections and asset values for impairment testing.

[ESRS 2 IRO-1 AR 13c] The Net Zero decarbonization scenario for Europe therefore focuses on the integration of various renewable energy sources and the improvement of energy ef ˱ciency. The plan includes a reduction in energy consumption, a signi˱cant increase in solar and wind power, and a strong increase in electricity storage capacity. Gas, which will be fully decarbonized, will be partially replaced by biomethane. Carbonfree hydrogen will also play a key role in transportation and industry.

ENGIE has several key convictions, including combining electrons and molecules for successful energy transition, the massive development of electricity generation from renewables, and the anticipation of ˳exibility needs. ENGIE has opted for a balanced mix, integrating renewable gas and carbon dioxide capture and storage in order to guarantee an energy system with the best levels of ef˱ciency and resilience.

[ESRS 2 IRO-1 AR 13d] The main limit of this prospective scenario, which by its nature contains uncertainties, concerns the role of green gas in future Net Zero energy systems and the capacity of countries to roll out renewables on a massive scale.

The model outputs from the central scenario determine the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions associated with the Group’s activities, the volume-based prices of energy and CO 2 , and energy demand. The results are compared with the model outputs of various recognized external scenarios, including those of grid operators (European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity – ENTSO-e, Réseau de Transport d’Électricité – RTE, Terna, National Grid, etc.), various government plans (National Energy and Climate Plan – NECP), or scenarios from public institutions (International Energy Agency – IEA, Agence de l'environnement et de la maîtrise de l'énergie – ADEME) or external consultants (AFRY, Aurora, Baringa).

[ESRS 2 IRO-1 AR 15] The scenarios used in the analysis are consistent with the assumptions used in the Group’s ˱nancial statements (see Section 3.1.2.1.5).

The Group carries out residual gas recovery services for its steel producing customer. These services meet a large part of its electricity needs, replacing the grid electricity required for the steelmaking process. The regulations in force require steel producers to burn process gases, which is usually done by industrial ˳aring. By converting the waste gases produced by its production processes into energy, ENGIE prevents these gases, representing a volume of 8 Mt CO 2 in 2025, from being ˳ared. ENGIE does not generate any additional CO 2 emissions in this recovery process. As the GHG Protocol does not take this speci ˱c case into account, ENGIE has chosen to apply the ISO14404:2024 standard - Calculation method of carbon dioxide emission intensity from iron and steel production, which con˱rms the steelmaker's responsibility for steel gases and their inclusion in its greenhouse gas emissions. Consequently, the Group excludes GHG emissions related to steel gases from its Scope 1 calculations for the three electricity generation facilities concerned: DK6 in France, and Knippegroen and Rodenhuize in Belgium.

This scope is supplemented by the contribution of entities accounted for using the equity method (associates and joint ventures). No cases have been identi˱ed in which ENGIE could have operational control according to the interpretation of the ESRS and the GHG Protocol, in entities not controlled by the Group.

As these are residual gases, a by-product, and not fuel with a supply chain, the Group does not include emissions from an upstream fuel chain in its Scope 3 emissions. The emissions related to the natural gas consumed in these facilities, in addition to steel gas when the latter is not suf˱cient to meet the industrial company's electricity needs, or at ENGIE's initiative when market conditions are favorable, are recorded in the Group's Scope 1.

Regarding pollution, consolidated analysis at Group head level identi ˱ed the following material IROs:

Policy in place [E2-1] [MDR-P]

[E2-1 15a, AR11] The Group has adopted a policy that aims to reduce and control the risks of pollution (air, water, soil) associated with its activities and value chain, and help protect people and ecosystems.

The policy includes approaches on:

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

• pollution prevention;

ENGIE endeavors to identify potential air, water and soil pollution generated by players upstream of its value chain through life-cycle assessments, to assess, for example, potential pollution in raw material extraction zones, which are often sources of environmental impact. This approach provides an overall vision of environmental impacts and a better understanding of the complete ecological footprint of the Group’s activities, from raw materials production to product and service end-of-life.

• the control process;

Incident and emergency management [ESRS E2-1 15c]

• incident and emergency management.

Prevention, reduction and control [ESRS E2-1 15a]

In the event of an emergency, detailed response procedures are in place, with specialized teams and management plans addressing each particular type of pollution. Regular training reinforces the Group’s ability to manage such situations effectively.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

To minimize the risk of air, water and soil pollution, ENGIE applies safety protocols and risk management strategies, including preventive maintenance and the use of best available techniques. These actions are underpinned by operational practices that enable the Group to avoid, control and monitor pollutant emissions. When emissions into the air, water and soil cannot be avoided, they are reduced for example by means of fume ˱ltration systems, pre-discharge water treatment or ground sealing systems.

If an incident occurs, immediate action is taken to limit its impact. This includes informing the affected communities, reducing emissions, and decontaminating the site. After an incident, ENGIE conducts investigations to determine the causes, repair any environmental and health damage, and implement corrective measures to avoid future incidents.

The presence of sites in water-stressed watersheds can also give rise to business opportunities, particularly in the context of water sharing. [MDR-A 68e] For example, in Chile, one of the thermal power plants located in an area of extreme water stress, which uses seawater, resells the desalinated water from its processes to a mine located in the middle of the desert, thus enabling it to limit its impact on freshwater resources. In 2025, 30,472,871 m 3 of water were sold to this third party.

• identify industrial sites subject to water stress. Every year, the Group’s ESG department assesses water-related risks using the Aqueduct tool (World Resource Institute) on the basis of the baseline water stress metric, with results made available to operational teams via a dedicated platform. For sites in areas of extreme or high water stress, local analysis is carried out by operational teams, who draw up action plans where appropriate, using an approach similar to that set in the Alliance for Water Stewardship standards, i.e., at site and watershed level, covering operational, regulatory and reputational aspects, and allowing for stakeholder and local context factors. In 2025, 175 sites were located in extreme water stress areas and 114 in high water stress areas. However, the Group evaluates proximity to areas containing threatened species, as de ˱ned by the IUCN Red List, for all sites, as part of its criteria for identifying material priority sites [SBM-3.16a].

List of material priority sites

[SBM-3 16a] The list of material priority sites for 2025, their breakdown by identi ˱ed impacts and dependencies, and the list of sensitive impacted areas are provided in Section 3.1.5.5 List of material priority sites. The ecological status is not consolidated at Group level.

[IRO-1 17ei, ii, iii] Mobilizing affected communities

Material priority sites are assessed according to ˱ve criteria, de˱ned according to ˱ve degrees of criticality. These criteria are as follows:

• proximity to protected areas: IUCN list (categories I to VI), Key Biodiversity Areas (KBA), Man and Biosphere Programme (MAB), World Database of Protected Areas (WDPA) including Ramsar and UNESCO world heritage sites (natural and mixed);

• IUCN Red List of Threatened Species;

In the course of its projects and operations, the Group carries out environmental and social impact analyses of its own activities to assess aspects such as the sustainability of biological resources and ecosystems. Locally, at a particular operating site or project, operational teams work to identify affected communities and establish dialogue to improve understanding of local issues and limit the impact on biodiversity and ecosystems. The feedback from dialogue with affected local communities provides input to the Group’s double materiality assessment.

• ecosystem integrity levels (according to the Globio model);

[IRO-1 19a] Impacted sites

• water stress zones;

The Group operated sites located in or near biodiversitysensitive areas. These sites are identi ˱ed using the Integrated Biodiversity Assessment Tool (IBAT), which enables access to various layers of global and national biological data, including data on sensitive areas. These sensitive areas are listed under the “proximity to protected areas” criterion in the “List of material priority sites” section.

• sector-based classi ˱cation of the impacts and dependencies of industrial activities. Here, the Group used the results of work on assessing the impacts and dependencies of the energy sector's activities on biodiversity. (Roadmap to Nature Positive: Foundations for the energy system) conducted by the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD), to which ENGIE contributed.

Material priority sites are determined as those with four or more “very high” criticality levels of these criteria.

Group operations affecting endangered species also use this platform to access data on threatened species listed in the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List.

[IRO-1 19b] Mitigation measures

Feedback from the ˱rst application of the methodology highlighted a need to integrate exclusion criteria to adapt effectively to realities on the ground. These criteria are as follows:

• activity type not applicable;

• the environmental impact study shows no impact on nature;

• absence of operational control of the site;

For projects, needs to implement mitigation measures are determined during the environmental and societal impact study. Such measures might, for example, involve programming the shutdown or ˳anging of wind turbines, or installing devices to prevent the nesting of certain species in construction zones.

• location in a highly urbanized area.

Mitigation measures at sites in operation involve ecological management such as late mowing, eco-grazing or zero pesticides.

[IRO-1 17b] Analysis of the biodiversity and ecosystem dependencies of the Group and its value chain

Resilience of the company’s biodiversity and ecosystem strategy and business model [E4-1]

This is based on the use of the LEAP method’s “Evaluate” process and the Biodiversity Footprint assessment ˱ndings using the Global Biodiversity Score tool.

Under the Group’s commitments, biodiversity and ecosystems are included as factors in its strategic planning and business model. ENGIE is strengthening such resilience in all its activities, especially as regards their main dependency, namely the availability of freshwater, as set out in Section 3.1.2.2.3 Water.

The Group has assessed its biodiversity dependencies sector by sector: gas storage and transport, gas distribution and marketing, thermal power production (by fuel type), wind power, solar power, biomass, hydroelectric power, geothermal power and water services (desalination). To do this, the Group used the WBCSD ˱ndings on the dependencies of the energy sector’s various activities on biodiversity.

Focus 3: Biodiversity and ecosystem matters in the value chain of Group activities

[E4-2 23d, 23e]

The Group is developing a methodology to evaluate the resilience of its activities to nature-related physical and transition risks. This methodology will be based on ENGIE’s strategic and operational data, coupled with the results of its footprint analyses and the LEAP methodology.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

A description of biodiversity-related impacts, risks and opportunities and their interactions with the Group’s strategy and business model appears in Section 3.1.1.4.2 “Material impacts, risks and opportunities”.

Through its Sustainable Procurement Policy, the Group prompts the inclusion of biodiversity factors throughout the value chain by exchanging with key suppliers and subcontractors and supporting them in nature-related challenges (see ENGIE’s Procurement Policy: https://www.engie.com/en/group/ suppliers/sustainable-purchasing-policy). The Group also promotes ecological transition among its customers.

Policy in place [E4-2]

Focus 4: Awareness-raising and knowledge-sharing

[MDR-P 65a] [E4-2 23a, 23b, 23c]

Biodiversity policy has four focuses:

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

Focus 1: Land footprint and ecological continuities

Awareness-raising and training are crucial to the effective take-up of biodiversity as an integrated factor in the development of Group activities. The Group runs e-learning training on the subject, plus the biodiversity fresk.

To reduce the land or aquatic footprint, contribute to the restoration of ecological corridors and reduce the presence of invasive alien species, the Group:

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

To include biodiversity protection as effectively as possible in the development of its activities, and contribute to the pursuance of knowledge on biodiversity both locally and internationally, the Group maintains and develops partnerships with biodiversity players, such as the French Committee of the IUCN and the UNEP World Conservation Monitoring Center at Group corporate level.

• implements an ecological site management approach, which aims to eliminate the use of chemical phytosanitary products, and which is based on maintenance practices that are adapted to the seasonal cycles of living organisms and promote local biodiversity;

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

It fosters the exchange of practices within its internal network of experts and practitioners, and supports and promotes operational initiatives aimed at developing innovative solutions that bene ˱t local communities throughout the life-cycle of its activities. In addition, ENGIE is working on measuring the biodiversity footprint of its activities, and on supporting PhD and research studies.

• locates protected areas and sensitive zones in the vicinity of its industrial sites, using tools made available to all employees, identi ˱es and quali˱es the proximity of its sites to determine, in consultation with local stakeholders, the most appropriate actions to minimize the impacts, or even transform them into positive impacts, while exploring innovative certi˱cation and ˱nancing tools;

[E4-2 23f]

• is committed to applying the avoid-reduce-compensate approach to project development worldwide.

Focus 2: Biodiversity and climate change

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

The biodiversity policy takes into account the consequences of impacts on the territories in which the Group operates, in line with its policy of stakeholder engagement (https:// www.engie.com/sites/default/ ˱les/assets/documents/202207/Stakeholders%20engagement%20policy_0.pdf), which include affected communities, local communities and indigenous peoples.

To help reduce the pressure on biodiversity caused by climate change, the Group has introduced a climate policy aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions from its own activities, and those of its customers and suppliers (see Section 3.1.2.1.2).

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

3.1.2.2.5 Resource use and circular economy [ESRS E5]

Introduction [IRO-1]

Policies, processes [E5-1]

The circular economy and natural resources policy was updated in 2024 and features eight key levers:

[ESRS E5 IRO-1 11a, 11b, AR 1-6] The double materiality assessment carried out at the head of the Group identi ˱ed the following impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs), broken down into three sub-topics.

1) A sub-topic on pressure on natural resources, with:

• eco-design: by encouraging eco-design, the Group can minimize the environmental and societal impacts of a product or industrial asset from the onset, reducing the use of new materials, including rare earths and critical materials for which there may be market tensions, possibly of a geopolitical nature, especially in the renewable energies sector;

• preserve: by reducing energy consumption (with a priority on energy sobriety and ef ˱ciency), the Group contributes to the preservation of natural resources;

• negative impact: pressure on resources, con ˳icts of use and geopolitical issues (e.g. competition with food for biomethane production, competition with wood, etc.), particularly for critical materials used by renewable energies in relation to impacts linked to resources [AR 7b] , or upkeep of the status quo, [AR 7c] or risks linked to the transition to a circular economy [AR 7e] ,

• positive impact: reduction in demand for resources resulting from (i) lower energy demand due to energy ef ˱ciency, (ii) eco-design of equipment and (iii) optimized operation of energy assets linked to circular economy opportunities [AR 7d] ,

• optimize: by combining, for example, its material, waste and energy ˳ows with those of neighbor partners, the Group can contribute to the emergence of a resourceef˱cient and cost-ef˱cient “industrial and territorial ecology”, in a win-win approach with its stakeholders, as with heat reuse or the call on local resources;

• risk: counterparty/supplier risk in the event of inability to honor contractual commitments on renewable energy projects owing to supply constraints regarding the resources used [AR 7b] and to maintaining the status quo [AR 7c] , or to risks regarding the transition to a circular economy [AR 7e] ,

• reuse: by reusing products or services, the Group reduces the production of waste or the use of natural resources, and contributes to the energy transition by adapting existing assets (converting gas networks to hydrogen, for example) that no longer meet the needs of an operating entity, or by recovering spare parts via a stock managed at Group level or during the dismantling of assets;

2) A sub-topic on the reuse of industrial assets with:

• repair: by repairing damaged or out-of-service products, such as used boilers or photovoltaic panels, the Group reduces the footprint of its activities while creating new jobs in the value chain;

• opportunity: the reuse and upgrading of Group infrastructure to support the energy transition (e.g., coal converted to biomass, gas networks adapted to hydrogen and biogas, wind turbines), in relation to material opportunities linked to the circular economy [AR 7d] ,

• opportunity: the strong demand for heating and cooling networks and methanization using local resources (biomass, geothermal energy, waste heat, manure, etc.), in relation to material opportunities linked to the circular economy [AR 7d] .

• recycle: by identifying appropriate recycling channels, particularly for renewable solar and wind energy and batteries, and stepping up recycling for waste generated by industrial activities and dismantling operations, the Group transforms waste into resources, thereby limiting the quantity of waste to be disposed of and the impact on natural resources;

3) A sub-topic on the dismantling of industrial assets with:

• risk: the increased costs for dismantling networks and treating the waste produced, regarding upkeep of the status quo [AR 7c] or the risks regarding the transition to a circular economy [AR 7e] .

• innovate: the Group is open to fresh approaches on strengthening the economy of resources, such as functionality economy (which prioritizes use rather than sale of a product), and provides innovative tools to support the decision-making process on the circular economy in industrial zones;

• empower: the Group uses resources sustainably through certi ˱ed or labeled channels (as for biomass).

[AR7a] The main entities concerned are: Renewables & Flex Power GBU for the ˱rst sub-topic; Networks GBU and Renewables & Flex Power GBU for the second; and, for the third, Electrabel, Renewables & Flex Power GBU and Local Energy Infrastructures.

Over the next few years, the Group’s businesses will be working to chart a circular economy roadmap in line with the Group’s policy.

Life-cycle assessment

[MDR-M 77a, 77b] Data can come from various sources. As a priority, ENGIE asks its suppliers for the necessary information. If they are unable to provide full data, data is drawn from internal databases and previous studies carried out by ENGIE. If data is still lacking, it is sought from bibliographic studies based on public data and from scienti ˱c literature and research.

[MDR-A 68e] Energy recovery - an example of action

For many years, ENGIE has been carrying out studies using the standardized LCA methodology. These studies cover the majority of the products and services provided by the Group (energy production using photovoltaic panels and wind turbines, energy storage using batteries, biomethane production, heating networks, etc.). They make it possible to assess the environmental impact at every stage of the life-cycle, from raw materials extraction through to product production, transport, use and end-of-life. This approach provides a comprehensive view of environmental impacts and helps identify opportunities for improvement and assessment.

LCA studies are carried out on an ongoing basis by a dedicated Group team, using the latest methodologies and tools. Previous LCAs are regularly updated to re ˳ect methodological advances and the latest data supplied by the Group or its suppliers.

In 2025, the Lesaffre group signed an agreement with ENGIE Solutions to install a new waste heat recovery unit at Lesaffre’s Marcq-en-Barœul plant. The entire project is based on complementarity all production stages. The purpose of the unit is to capture the heat generated on site, currently dissipated into the air via cooling towers, and redirect it to another production stage requiring heat, which is currently provided by a gas- ˱red boiler. Speci˱cally, two heat pumps with a total capacity of 19 MWth will be installed to recover the heat produced in the fermentation process during the yeast cell multiplication stage and enable it to be used in another production process at the plant, drying the yeast. In addition to reducing CO 2 emissions, this system will also reduce the site’s water consumption by around 150,000 m³ of water per year.

The Material Risks Passport

ENGIE does not currently have speci ˱c Group-wide targets for minimizing the use of natural resources or increasing the use of recycled resources. The Group will continue applying its Material Risk Passport to other technologies to prepare for this identi˱cation process.

In addition to LCA studies covering environmental impact in all value chains, ENGIE is currently working on rollout of the Material Risks Passport, to identify the risks involved in the consumption of natural resources in energy production and storage technologies. The aim is to closely identify and assess the risks associated with resources. The methodology covers aspects including: availability/scarcity of raw materials, criticality of materials, substitutability of materials, geopolitical risks, societal risks and traceability of materials. It also meets the requirements of Article 24 of the European Regulation of April 11, 2024, setting a framework to ensure secure and sustainable supply of critical raw materials in terms of business risk preparedness.

[MDR-A 68e] The Passport seeks improved understanding and anticipation of the risks associated with the raw materials used in the Group’s technologies, thereby facilitating proactive supply management. Since 2024, a total of nine technologies have been studied, four of which were added or updated in 2025, covering ˱ve activity families: solar, wind, batteries, electrolyzers and power grids. As well as helping to minimize risks, this initiative also strengthens the Group’s position in an economy increasingly focused on sustainability and

[E5-3 24c, AR17] To evaluate the criticality of renewable technologies, the Group continued to roll out its Material Risk Passport. In 2025, risks were studied for two new technologies – an inverter and a transformer – alongside an update for the photovoltaic sector. The photovoltaic update improved the “TOPCon Bifacial” case study initiated in 2024 in partnership with the CEA (French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission) and the INES (National Institute for Solar Energy). This enabled the supplementation of literature-based data with operational data and made several points of the Bill of Materials (BOM) parametric. The BOM covers essential elements of the production process, from design to production and product assembly. This broadens the scope of the case studies conducted to date.

Note on the dismantling of nuclear power plants in Belgium

Note on the dismantling of non-nuclear sites

[MDR-A 68e] There was no signi ˱cant dismantling activity in 2025.

The reactors concerned are currently in the ˱nal shutdown phase, which comprises four stages: unloading of the reactor and transfer of the nuclear fuel to the deactivation pools, decontamination of the primary circuit, evacuation of the fuel to temporary storage buildings, then evacuation of the ˱lters and resins, ˱nal rinsing of the circuits and pools, and evacuation of waste, ef˳uents and hazardous products.

Once dismantling operations are suf˱ciently advanced, and if the permit so allows, Electrabel will start dismantling the installations in 2028, according to the current schedule. Dismantling activities in the reactor building will determine the duration of this phase.

[MDR-A 68a, b] Given the growing importance of access to critical materials needed for renewable energies, and the challenges of managing end-of-life of assets in the years ahead, an end-of-life strategy is of crucial importance for each country in the Renewable & Flex Power GBU. Key points of this strategy concern the structure of the GBU’s approach to dismantling wind and solar farms, and the implementation of an environmentally-conscious method for managing the growing volumes in the years ahead. This means anticipating and mitigating the ˱nancial risks involved in asset dismantling, ensuring effective cost management, identifying potential risks, and complying with regulations.

The main principles applied by this GBU are:

• zero land ˱ll: land˱ll must be avoided for all dismantled renewable energy assets;

• environmentally-sound dismantling: dismantling practices must minimize environmental impact and disruption to ecosystems and local communities; all hazardous materials must be disposed of safely, in compliance with local and international regulations;

All dismantling operations at nuclear installations are subject to the safety imperatives set by the Federal Agency for Nuclear Control (FANC). This dedicated legal structure is consolidated using the equity method, which excludes it from the scope of the Taxonomy. Henceforth, only drawing rights on French power plants identi˱ed as Taxonomy-eligible by EDF will also be identi˱ed as eligible by the Group.

Non-eligible activities mainly relate to sales of electricity and gas as a marketer (1) or trader), as these activities are currently excluded from the scope of the Taxonomy.

In order to direct European industrial investments toward sustainable activities and achieve carbon neutrality by 2050, the European Union has established a regulatory framework by adopting Regulation No. 2020/852 of June 18, 2020 and the adoption of four delegated acts – (2021/2139) dated June 4, 2021, (2022/1214) dated March 9, 2022 and (2023/2485 and 2023/2486) dated June 27, 2023 – a European Taxonomy that de ˱nes the economic activities deemed environmentally sustainable. The adoption on July 4, 2025 of Delegated Regulation 2026/73 introduced simplifying measures applied by the ENGIE Group. These measures ease the generic Do No Signi˱cant Harm (DNSH) criteria regarding pollution prevention and reduction, and simplify the models for reporting indicators. In 2026, the Group will study the application of materiality thresholds to exclude non-material activities.

The second stage consisted of determining, among the eligible activities, those that made a substantial contribution to the climate change mitigation or adaptation objective by assessing their compliance with the technical review criteria presented in the delegated acts. The life-cycle assessment criterion of 100 g CO 2 /kWh does not currently qualify the Group’s natural gas- ˱red power generation assets on its own. Among the technical review criteria, the activity is considered aligned if:

• for hydropower generation: the hydropower plant was a “run of the river” type or can demonstrate a power ˳ux density of more than 5 W/m 2 – certain large capacity hydropower installations are therefore not aligned for this reason;

The Group followed a four-step process to identify the activities which are eligible and aligned in accordance with the European Regulation governing the Taxonomy of sustainable activities (2020/852) across all the countries where the Group operates. For Taxonomy-eligible activities, the process covered all six Taxonomy objectives: the two climate objectives concerning climate change mitigation and adaptation as well as the four other environmental objectives: sustainable use and protection of water and marine resources, transition to a circular economy, pollution prevention and control, and protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems.

• for the heating networks: the energy system was ef ˱cient as de˱ned by the EU (using at least 50% renewables, 50% residual heat, 75% cogenerated heat or 50% a combination of such energy and heat);

• for the installation of energy ef ˱ciency equipment or energy performance services in the buildings: the activity is related to one of the activities described.

The analysis of economic activities across all six objectives shows that the Group is mainly concerned with the mitigation objective, in line with its purpose and its decarbonization strategy (see Section 3.1.5.6 Taxonomy tables). Activities related to other objectives, which are not material with regard to the indicators covered by the European Taxonomy, are therefore implicitly included in the mitigation objective declared for the Group.

The third stage related to compliance with technical review criteria ensuring no detriment to the other environmental objectives (Do No Signi ˱cant Harm – DNSH). Risk management relating to climate change, water resources, the circular economy, the erosion of biodiversity and air pollution is covered by ENGIE’s environmental policies (see ESRS E1 to E5 and the Group’s website: https://www.engie.com/en/group/ social-responsibility/csr-goals). The compliance assessment was carried out by environmental coordinators for each activity based on the following main elements:

• the analysis of risks relating to climate change (physical risks), water stress, pollution (NOx, SOx, PM), the conservation of protected areas which is updated each year as part of environmental reporting on sites in operation;

• the preparation of an environmental management plan as part of the Group’s voluntary ESG objectives;

• EMAS (1) and ISO 14001 certi ˱cation for installations with the highest environmental impact such as hydropower production sites.

The ˱rst stage consisted of studying the eligibility of activities and dividing the Group’s economic activities into two categories: eligible and non-eligible. To do so, the Group determined which of its activities strictly corresponded to an economic activity described in one of the delegated acts (2021/2139), (2022/1214) or (2023/2486). The primary activities identi ˱ed as eligible are Renewable & BESS (wind, solar, hydro, geothermal electricity production and storage), Gas Generation (fossil-fuel electricity production) and Local Energy Infrastructures (heat production and distribution with or without gas or biomass cogeneration, energy ef˱ciency services). For the Networks scope, activities relating to the greening of injected, transported and distributed natural gas were taken into account in proportion to the green gas transported in the networks (activities 4.9 – Transmission and distribution of electricity and 4.14 – Transport and distribution networks for renewable and low-carbon gas). This section describes the Group’s human rights approach and applies to all the material negative human rights impacts identi ˱ed in the framework of the double materiality assessment, informed by the risks identi˱ed via the vigilance process (see Section 3.2 Vigilance Plan for more information).

ENGIE believes that human rights are fundamental to the just energy transition to which it aspires and which lies at the heart of its purpose. ENGIE’s activities have a positive impact on many people and contribute to the development of the regions in which the Group operates. In particular, ENGIE provides access to energy and creates jobs in the countries where the Group operates. However, the positive impact ENGIE seeks to achieve can only be created if the rights of those affected by the company’s operations and value chain are upheld.

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

All IROs relating to own workforce, value chain workers, affected communities and consumers and end-users are described in Section 3.1.1.4.2. These IROs, along with the Group’s speci˱c commitments, policies, actions, targets and metrics are described in the sections on own workforce (Section 3.1.3.2), workers in the value chain (Sections 3.1.3.3 and 3.1.3.4), affected communities (Section 3.1.3.5) and consumers and end-users (Section 3.1.3.6).

The Group’s human rights commitments

ENGIE undertakes to (i) uphold the human rights of all individuals and groups potentially affected by its activities and (ii) ensure that its activities are conducted in compliance with the highest standards of protection and, at a minimum, in accordance with the provisions of international laws protecting and defending human rights. These commitments are set out in the Group’s Human Rights Vigilance Policy.

Respect for human rights is central to ENGIE’s Ethics Code of Conduct, its policies, especially its Human Rights Vigilance Policy, and its Vigilance Plan (see Section 3.2.), which was drawn up in accordance with French law on the duty of vigilance of parent companies and ordering companies. The Group’s human rights commitments are also part of the Group’s social dialogue, particularly in the context of ENGIE’s Global Framework Agreement on Fundamental Rights and Social Responsibility, which was signed in January 2022. (see Section 3.1.3.2.3 Working conditions and social dialogue). This Agreement can be consulted at the following address: https://www.engie.com/en/news/international-social-agreement.

This section describes in greater detail the Human Rights Vigilance Policy and the Just Transition Policy which apply across the different social information sections.

Human Rights Vigilance Policy

Various resources, including the Ethics Code of Conduct (available on the Group’s website in 15 languages), training courses and handbooks (guide on combating sexual harassment and sexist acts), have been deployed to raise employee awareness of human rights matters, duty of vigilance responsibilities and the Group’s Whistleblowing System.

More information on the human rights vigilance approach is available at: https://www.engie.com/en/group/ethics-and-compliance/ policies-and-procedures/human-rights-referential.

[MDR-P] The purpose of ENGIE’s Human Rights Vigilance Policy is to de ˱ne the Group’s human rights commitments and the means to ensure they are upheld. This policy is the foundation of the Group’s vigilance approach for human rights.

Group policies

It aims to identify, prevent and manage risks of human rights violations against all persons throughout the ENGIE value chain, particularly workers, communities, users and clients. It also seeks to ensure that human rights incidents are dealt with effectively.

[S1-1 21, S2-1 19, S3-1 17, S4-1 17] ENGIE’s policies are aligned with internationally recognized standards pertaining to own workforce, value chain workers, affected communities and consumers and end-users, especially the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights.

To ensure compliance with its human rights commitments, meet regulatory requirements and manage the Group’s human rights challenges, the Group relies ˱rst and foremost on its Human Rights Vigilance Policy – a cornerstone policy that covers all the potential negative impacts of its activities on people.

Just Transition Policy

CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C CH1C

A just transition therefore means managing restructuring in a responsible manner by creating a common set of guarantees for employees affected by a plant closure and helping them to improve their employability through skills development. It also means contributing to the economic and social vitality of host regions by creating projects and supplying affordable energy. Lastly, it helps make the regions more resilient and less vulnerable by preserving natural resources and local communities.

The Just Transition Policy is an integral part of the Group’s purpose. The notion of a “just transition” stems from the belief that a shift to a sustainable, lower-carbon economy can only take place if social concerns are taken into account. The transition should be conducted in a way that is fair to all stakeholders – own workforce, value chain workers, affected communities, consumers and end-users – and strive to minimize the negative effects, while maximizing the positive ones.

Interests and views of Group employees

[SBM-2 12] The Group's employees are one of the eight stakeholder categories identi ˱ed by ENGIE. The Group tailors its dialogue based on their speci˱c needs (see Section 3.1.1.2.3 Interests and views of stakeholders [SBM-2]).

Every two years, the ENGIE&Me internal survey anonymously collects employees’ views on their relationship with the company and their perception of how their interests are considered in the Group’s strategy. The engagement of the Group’s employees has remained constant or improved since 2022, reaching a sustainable engagement rate of 87% in 2024. The next survey will take place in 2026, allowing time to roll out, at team and/or entity level, the action plans decided following the previous survey.

Material IROs and their interaction with ENGIE’s strategy and business model [SBM-3]

[SBM-3 14e] ENGIE supports the transformation towards more environmentally friendly operations, contributing to the global carbon neutrality objective. Against the backdrop of restructuring to support the energy transition of fossil fuel–related activities, the Group seeks to anticipate and mitigate potential social impacts on its employees. This transformation involves certain risks, including “potential job losses resulting from changes in ENGIE’s business model, evolving labor market dynamics, and the introduction of disruptive technologies such as generative AI”. It can also result in a “mismatch between available skills and new needs, leading to shortages of quali ˱ed personnel and the loss of key know-how in the event of departures or geographical mobility” (see Section 3.1.1.4.2 Material impacts, risks and opportunities). Recognizing these challenges, ENGIE also sees this transformation as an opportunity to create jobs and strengthen the skills of its employees. By investing in training, the Group supports the employability and professional development of its teams.

The results of the double materiality assessment re ˳ect the important role of employees in the Group’s strategy. Four positive impacts, ˱ve negative impacts and six material risks were identi˱ed. They are listed in Section 3.1.1.4.2 of this Sustainability Statement.

Processes [S1-2]

A standardized methodology guarantees the consistency of consolidated social data, their comparability between entities and their relevance on an international scale. De ˱nitions, sources and scopes are harmonized in a common Group reference system through an operational manual shared with all entities.

Social dialogue at different levels of the Group

Collection tool

[S1-2 27a, b, c] In recent years, the Group has developed a robust culture of social dialogue at all levels of the organization. The social dialogue bodies regularly present the strategic orientations of the Group, the GBU and/or the entity to trigger the exchanges necessary for their adoption. Transformation and/or restructuring projects are also presented before a ˱nal decision is made and the project goes ahead, in accordance with local legislation.

For local entities and subsidiaries controlled by the Group, with the exception of a few companies, social data on employee ˳ows and training are collected daily from a centralized global HR information system. These consolidated data are reported quarterly in the Group social reporting via a dedicated consolidation tool. It centralizes data on ˱xed and variable pay, contractual hours and part of the bene˱ts in kind of employees of the Group. However, it cannot be used to create a single database containing individual pay data for each employee.

• at local level: within the entities, on a frequent and multi-year basis, with trade unions and/or employee representatives and local management representatives, at the most relevant level (company, business unit, region, site, etc.);

Information on working conditions and contingent workers is reported directly by the entities on a quarterly basis via the same social data consolidation tool.

• at country level: one to two meetings are held each year between the country manager and the country employee representatives; in France, these meetings take place within the framework of the French Group Works Council, a joint body at Group level;

For the regulated entities (GRDF, NaTran and CNR), due to regulatory requirements that limit the pooling of their information systems with the rest of the Group, the entirety of their social data is entered via the consolidation tool on a quarterly basis.

Quantitative data collection process

The governance of social metrics is based on a clear, hierarchical organization:

• at European level : the European Works Council (EWC) is endowed with prerogatives aligned with European regulations, although they have not yet been transposed into French law. The EWC has supra-legal resources and is speci ˱cally consulted in a multi-year cycle in particular on the Group’s orientations (see targets and metrics in this section);

• local level: each subsidiary is responsible for collecting social data in accordance with the guidelines and tools provided by the Group;

• at global level: a forum for dialogue, the Global Forum, chaired by the Group’s Chief Executive Of ˱cer, meets annually in the presence of international federations and their designated members.

• regional level: data are reviewed and validated by regional coordinators from each relevant part of the world to ensure their quality and compliance with standards;

• Group level: data are centralized and the metrics analyzed at Group level, before being submitted to the Group’s departments and committees.

As part of the Group’s transformation, regular and extraordinary meetings are scheduled to allow employee representatives to issue informed recommendations and opinions as necessary. Thematic working groups (e.g., social issues, health & safety) are also organized among members.

Global Agreement

3.1.3.2.3 Working conditions and social dialogue [S1–1, S1-2, S1-4, S1-5, S1-8, S1-10, S1-11, S1-15]

Social dialogue [S1-2, S1-4, S1-5, S1-8]

In its various forms (informal exchanges, discussions, negotiations, consultations, etc.), social dialogue between the Group and its employees, either directly or through their representatives, is both a driver of economic performance and an essential element of ENGIE’s strategy.

[S1-2 27d] The Group, international federations and French trade unions negotiated and signed an agreement in January 2022 on ENGIE’s fundamental rights and social responsibility. This agreement (“Global Agreement”) incorporates the expectations of the workforce as expressed by employee representatives and applies to the Group’s workforce worldwide, regardless of the type of employment contract.

Such dialogue makes it possible to gather the views of employees and integrate them into the Group’s developments in order to improve working conditions for the entire workforce. Explaining, clarifying and discussing the Group’s policies, transformations and restructuring projects and their impacts on employees are essential steps in their implementation.

The Global Agreement contains commitments on ethics and duty of vigilance, anti-harassment, safety, workplace well-being, diversity and inclusion, skills development and training, and more. It enables the application of high standards in terms of labor relations and workers’ rights through regular, open and constructive social dialogue at all levels. The Global Forum mentioned above is a social dialogue forum responsible for monitoring and implementing commitments de ˱ned under this agreement.

Whether it takes place within the institutional framework of mandatory negotiations (including on wages, working hours or restructuring) or spontaneously and constructively, social dialogue is an essential means of preventing tensions and con ˳icts and in that way contributes directly to preventing

Gender equality is one of the pillars of the Group’s DEI Policy. ENGIE aims to achieve a gender balance with 40-60% women in management at Group level by 2030. In 2022, in line with its commitments and for greater clarity, the Group decided that it would focus on the equal pay metric from among the gender and pay equity metrics. It measures the difference between the pay of women and men in equivalent positions.

The calculation is therefore based on average Full-Time Equivalent pay, which can be calculated from GSR data and which excludes the highest-paid individual.

The elements of pay taken into account are the base salary, variable pay and individual and collective bonuses. The following items are excluded: ˱xed-term contract termination bene˱ts, bonuses linked to service requirements, overtime and additional hours worked, severance payments, seniority bonuses, incentives and pro˱t-sharing, shares and deferred share-based payments.

Health & Safety Policy

ENGIE’s Health & Safety Policy is based on eight fundamental principles, such as taking risks into account in all decisionmaking processes, a participatory approach to the prevention of hazardous situations and the promotion of a climate of trust and dialogue.

[MDR-P 65a] ENGIE’s approach to health & safety at work includes two distinct prevention axis:

• “No Life At Risk”, which deals with accident prevention;

• “No Mind At Risk”, which focuses on improving quality of life at work and preventing psychosocial risks.

A reviewed version of this policy was published in 2022 in conjunction with the introduction of a Global Framework Agreement on Fundamental Rights and ENGIE’s Social Responsibility. This revision made it possible to introduce the No Mind at Risk prevention axis and additional practical provisions intended to improve quality of life at work and prevent psychosocial risks.

These two prevention axes are de ˱ned in the Health & Safety Policy, which was the subject of a global agreement with employee representatives.

The Group’s ambition, expressed in the preamble to its policy, is to make everyone – executives, managers, employees, subcontractors – a committed actor in their own health & safety, and that of others.

[MDR-P] Health & Safety Policy
